Context-Free Rewriting Systems (CFRs) extend Context-Free Grammars (CFGs) by allowing non-terminals to be replaced with complex patterns. While a single-headed CFR is known to generate tree languages closed under the tree inverse homomorphism operation, this note demonstrates that CFRs equipped with multiple heads can achieve greater power. Specifically, we present a minimal example of a two-headed CFR that produces a language outside the class closed under the tree inverse homomorphism operation. This construction relies on a two-headed CFR with only one non-terminal. Furthermore, we establish that any two-headed CFR capable of producing such a counterexample language must also possess at least one non-terminal.

We investigate the potential for a rotational direction asymmetry in galaxies by analyzing the distribution of 10,000 galaxies from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) in the Northern Hemisphere. Our results indicate a slight excess of clockwise rotations, though this is not statistically significant. We also contrast our findings with data from four other sky surveys: the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey, the 6dF Galaxy Survey, and the SDSS-III Main Galaxy Sample. The latter three surveys cover the Southern Hemisphere, allowing us to compare rotation trends across both hemisshpheres. We find a marginally higher frequency of clockwise galaxies in the Southern Hemisphere, but this difference remains statistically insignificant. We further demonstrate that the observed asymmetry is not driven by the orientation of the Northern or Southern Galactic Poles.

Meta-learning has proven highly effective in low-data regimes, yet practical applications often involve noisy labels and sampling errors. This paper introduces REptainE (Eigen-Reptile), a method that integrates label noise and sampling noise perturbations into meta-optimization. By employing a meta-optimization framework, REptainE learns a robust initialization that minimizes the impact of these perturbations, thereby enhancing generalization. The core mechanism involves iteratively updating the initialization using second-order derivatives of the meta-loss, which are computed via eigen-decomposition of the Hessian matrix. This approach offers two key advantages: it significantly reduces computational overhead compared to full Hessian calculations, and it enables the use of large batch sizes to improve the stability of meta-optimization. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-100 demonstrate that REptainE outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both standard and perturbed meta-learning scenarios. The project's code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenruiZhang/Eigen-Reptile.

We introduce ICAM-reg, a novel interpretable framework for brain imaging that integrates the strengths of both feature selection and end-to-end learning. This approach identifies the most relevant features for predicting continuous outcomes, such as cognitive scores, while simultaneously learning optimal feature weights. By employing a novel attribution technique, the model generates per-sample feature importance scores, offering a clear and intuitive understanding of the model's decisions. This capability facilitates the detection of individual-level anomalies, like those seen in Alzheimer's disease, and allows for the creation of personalized brain age estimators. Furthermore, ICAM-REG supports multi-site analysis by enabling the model to adapt to varying imaging protocols.

This paper investigates moral development within artificial intelligence systems, specifically examining the ethical dimensions of the "margins"—the boundaries and peripheries of AI design. It argues that the moral integrity of an AI is contingent not only on its core moral algorithms but also on how it integrates the marginal data sets used for training. By analyzing contemporary developments in AI morality, we demonstrate that current research frequently overlooks these marginal aspects, thereby failing to fully grasp how an AI's moral conduct emerges. Consequently, this paper advocates for a more rigorous examination of how marginal influences shape AI morality, suggesting that future research must account for these marginal factors to effectively ensure the moral safety of intelligent machines.

The extent of a language refers to the smallest collection of regular languages required to represent it as a union. This paper examines the properties of these extents specifically for $\mathfrak{o}$-regular languages, which are defined as $\mathfrak{o}$-recursive sets within $\mathfrak{o}$-recursive spaces. We demonstrate that for any $\mathfrak{o}$-regular language, the extent is itself an $\mathfrak{o}$-recursive set. Furthermore, we establish that the collection of all such extensive $\mathfrak{o}$-regular languages is closed under finite unions, intersection, and complementation. Finally, we outline the decidability of determining whether a given $\mathfrak{o}$-recursive set can be expressed as a union of a countable family of regular languages.

This study introduces a deep learning-based framework for channel assessment and forecasting within cell-free massive-input multiple-output (mMIMO) systems, accounting for channel degradation. The proposed method utilizes a recurrent neural network (RNN) to model channel evolution over time and employs a convolutional neural network (CNN) to capture spatial dependencies among access points. By integrating these components, the system generates a comprehensive channel state information (CSI) representation that facilitates accurate CSI estimation and future prediction. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing CSI estimation techniques, particularly in scenarios involving channel degradation.

This study examines the impact of lattice QCD calculations on the determination of the CKM matrix element $V_{ud}$ within superallowed $0^+ \to 0^+$ nuclear $\beta$-decays. We investigate how accounting for short-distance radiative corrections, specifically the $V-A$ operator renormalization and the Sirlin term $B_{NS}$, influences this determination. By employing recent lattice QCD results for $B_{NS}$, we demonstrate that the resulting shift in $V_{ud}$ is substantial, reaching approximately $1.5 \times 10^{-4}$.

This study introduces Identity Augmented Residual Image Denoising (ARIAD), a novel deep neural network architecture designed to denoise images. A key component of ARIAD is the Identity-Mapping-Block (IMB), which facilitates the direct transmission of clean image features from input to output, thereby accelerating training and enhancing performance. Additionally, ARIAD employs a residual image denoising (RiD) approach, leveraging the fact that the difference between a noisy and a clean image—termed the residual—is significantly less complex than the original clean image. This allows the network to concentrate on modeling these simpler residual features rather than reconstructing the entire clean image. This strategy effectively reduces computational costs and improves performance. The proposed architecture is highly efficient, requiring only 0.02M parameters to achieve a PSNR of 31.6 dB on the Gaussian white noise dataset, outperforming the state-of-the-art DnCNN by 0.6 dB.

Correlation-driven approaches, including self-supervised learning and self-supervised guidance, have proven highly effective in computer vision. However, their theoretical underpinnings remain unclear. This study introduces a new framework for understanding these methods by analyzing the identifiability of the underlying representation. We demonstrate that when a model incorporates latent correlations between views, self-supervised learning can recover these views up to a specific permutation and scaling factor. Furthermore, we establish the identifiability of self-guided self-supervised fine-tuning, showing that the refined model preserves the necessary correlations to maintain view consistency. Our theoretical findings are substantiated by experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

We introduce a novel sample of 100 galaxies exhibiting extreme mid-infrared (MIR) dust colours, defined by the ratio of flux at 24 to 8 microns ($f_{24}/f_8$) exceeding 10. This selection is based on the Spitzer Space Telescope's Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) data. By analyzing the MIR spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of these sources, we determine that approximately 70% of the sample are dominated by star formation, while the remaining 30% are characterized by intense starbursts. The majority of these galaxies are located at redshifts $z > 1.5$, and they are notably reddier than typical star-forming systems at similar redshifts. These findings suggest that the sample consists largely of star-forming galaxies with unusually high MIR dust temperatures. We also observe a strong correlation between MIR colour and the ratio of MIR to optical luminosity ($L_{24}/L_{\rm opt}$), indicating that MIR colours serve as a reliable indicator of star formation activity in these galaxies.

Ethical decision-making is a critical component of human behavior, and moral exceptions are essential for creating nuanced judgments in complex situations. For instance, a doctor might violate confidentiality to prevent harm, or a bystander might intervene in an assault to protect a victim. Despite this, current moral decision frameworks struggle to account for such exceptions, often relying on rigid, rule-based systems that fail to capture necessary flexibility. This study investigates how pre-trained language models (PLMs) handle scenarios involving moral exceptions, using them as a proxy to simulate human behavior. We introduce the Moral Exception Benchmark (MEB), which assesses PLMs' ability to identify and justify these exceptions across various contexts. Our results indicate that PLMs can effectively recognize exceptions in certain domains but struggle with others, suggesting that these models reflect human moral reasoning by incorporating exceptions. Furthermore, we observe that PLMs are more likely to justify exceptions when they involve negative outcomes, mirroring a human tendency to prioritize minimizing harm over strict rule adherence.

We demonstrate that the class of valuation domains (including those that are finite-type over a field) can be expressed as directed unions of complete rings of integer convergence. Conversely, the class of valuation domains exhibiting a finite character is representable as such unions in relation to quadratic convergence complexes. In both instances, the resulting systems are constructed through completions of localized polynomial rings defined over a universal base field.

This study addresses the challenges of numerically solving the Dirac equation in two dimensions, specifically for a particle interacting with an external potential. We begin by deriving the associated time-evolution equation and the corresponding Schrödinger equation, which is then utilized to formulate a standard Crank-Nicolson numerical scheme. However, this approach is shown to be impractical due to its reliance on a nonlinear algebraic equation. To overcome this, we derive a simplified Crank-Nicolkinson scheme specifically for one-dimensional systems, which is then extended to two dimensions using a finite difference method. We further demonstrate that applying the Fourier pseudospectral technique yields a significantly more efficient solution. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the proposed methods.

This study investigates Collaborative Adaptive Cruise Control and vehicle platooning using a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework. The approach relies on a communication network to share velocity data among neighboring vehicles within a platoon. The analysis evaluates how communication disruptions influence platoon stability and the system's sensitivity to various network topologies. The findings indicate that MPC-based collaborative Adaptive Cruise Control and platooning offer significant potential for enhancing traffic flow efficiency and safety.

In recent years, the reliability of information on social networking sites has become increasingly critical. While users often rely on experts or trusted individuals to verify news, this strategy is impractical given the massive number of users on platforms like Twitter. Consequently, there is a pressing need for a mechanism that enables users to gauge the credibility of all Twitter accounts. This study introduces a system designed to assess Twitter user reliability by leveraging a user-driven approach that integrates both viewing habits and explicit trust relationships. By utilizing a graph-based model, the system calculates trust scores for all accounts. Furthermore, the research evaluates the system's performance through a comprehensive analysis of the credibility of viewing and trusted users, alongside an empirical assessment of how closely the calculated trust scores align with actual user perceptions of reliability.

In vehicular environments, time-critical events often demand immediate attention, such as a vehicle detecting a stalled car on a highway and instantly alerting following drivers. To ensure these alerts reach drivers before they reach the hazard, data must be gathered and processed rapidly. However, the sporadic and unpredictable nature of these incidents makes it difficult to predict when and where they will occur, rendering traditional static data collection methods ineffective. To address this, we introduce $\pi$-ROAD, a novel, learn-as-you-go framework designed to dynamically select vehicles for data acquisition. This approach leverages historical data to forecast where urgent events are likely to happen and identifies which cars are optimally positioned to collect them. By integrating a reinforcement learning agent with a distributed computing architecture, $\pi$-ROAD continuously refines its selection strategy as the network expands. Simulation results indicate that $\pi$-ROAD surpasses existing methods in both coverage and efficiency, achieving a 20% increase in urgent event coverage and a 30% reduction in the number of vehicles required for data collection.

The advancement of the Industry 4.0 has spurred the development of collaborative robots (cobots) designed to operate safely alongside humans. However, current cobots lack the capability to learn complex tasks from human demonstrations. This paper introduces CoHaptics, a novel human-robot collaboration framework that enables cobots to acquire skills from various physical interaction methods, including hand gestures and arm movements. The system utilizes a haptic feedback interface to inform the operator of a cobot's proximity, while a collaborative robot executes the learned task. To ensure safety, the proposed system incorporates a collision avoidance mechanism that halts operations when the distance between the human and the robot falls below a defined threshold. Experimental evaluations were conducted to validate the system's effectiveness.

This study introduces a new socio-technical framework for analyzing city governance, grounded in the concepts of independence and mobility. Drawing upon established theories of governance, we examine how urban systems function as interconnected entities, emphasizing the critical role of institutions in facilitating effective city management.

This paper examines online caching within a network where request patterns are partially observable. We propose a novel framework that leverages machine learning to generate predictions of future demands, which are subsequently integrated into online caching policies. Our primary objective is to minimize the average long-term cost of evicted data by strategically utilizing these predictions. We introduce a new class of stochastic online caching problems and develop a corresponding algorithm, demonstrating that it achieves a finite competitive ratio under the assumption of perfect machine accuracy. Furthermore, we analyze the algorithm's robustness against prediction errors, proving that its competitive ratio remains bounded as long as prediction errors are sufficiently small. Finally, we apply this methodology to a specific caching scenario, showing that our approach yields significant performance gains over traditional methods when prediction accuracy is high.

Deep learning has become a standard for medical image segmentation, yet most current methods rely on a simple encoder-decoder framework that often fails to capture long-range dependencies, resulting in poor segmentation of small objects. This study addresses this limitation by introducing a novel Trilateral Focus Network (TFN) designed to enhance the encoder's ability to extract long-range contextual information. TFN integrates a novel attention mechanism that combines a long-range feature aggregation module with a short-range feature aggregation module. This dual-aggregation approach allows the network to effectively fuse both local and global features, thereby improving the segmentation of small objects. Furthermore, the network includes a new adaptive sampling module to enhance the training process. Comprehensive evaluations on public benchmarks demonstrate that TFN achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the network is optimized for real-time applications, delivering high-quality segmentation results with minimal latency.

This study examines the local off-shell formulation of eleven-dimensional supergravity, representing the linearized theory of supergravity within the framework of 4+7 supergeometry. We establish the linearized theory as a gauge-invariant theory of gauge fields defined on a linear superspace that constitutes a gauge transformation of a neighborhood within an off-shell 4+7 supermanifold. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the gauge-invariant group of these gauge fields forms a subgroup of the supergroup of diffeomorphisms of this linearized space, which is itself a subset of the supergroup of diffeomorphisms of the original off-shell 4+7 supermanifold.

Data quality is fundamental to the success of data-driven projects, yet the inherent diversity of these assets makes their assessment and enhancement inherently difficult. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages the training dynamics of Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDTs) to evaluate and improve data quality. The method employs a sequential training strategy using GBDT variants, where each iteration incorporates a subset of the data. By analyzing the training loss across these sequential models, we can identify and address specific data quality issues. We validate this approach on synthetic datasets and compare it against established metrics, demonstrating its effectiveness in evaluating and refining data quality.

Large-scale denoising pretraining of pretrained language models (PLMs) has recently gained traction due to its ability to generate high-quality embeddings for downstream NLP tasks. This approach involves reconstructing corrupted input sentences by predicting missing tokens. However, the quality of these embeddings is heavily dependent on the PLM's capacity to identify which corrupted tokens are genuinely useful for recovery. To address this, we introduce a novel pretraining strategy that leverages the PLM itself to identify high-quality tokens for denoising. Specifically, we utilize a combination of the PLM's internal attention weights and output probabilities to select tokens for reconstruction. Our findings demonstrate that this approach significantly enhances the quality of generated embeddings. Furthermore, the resulting models achieve state-of-the-art performance across various downstream tasks, including sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, and question answering.

Quantum networks are a foundational element for the future of quantum information processing, yet their construction is currently constrained by the scarcity of functional nodes and limited inter-node connectivity. Consequently, it is essential to determine the topology of these networks using the fewest available nodes. This work introduces a methodology to infer quantum network structure by measuring local observables at an individual node, enabling the reconstruction of the entire system's architecture. We demonstrate that this approach allows for the determination of the quantum state within a network, even when only a single node is accessible. Furthermore, we show that the proposed method can identify the topology of a quantum network, regardless of whether the nodes share entangled or product states. Finally, we outline how the technique can be extended to uncover the topology of general high-dimensional quantum networks.

Information visualizations are widely used to convey data insights, yet they can be challenging for novices to understand. This difficulty stems from the need to interpret both the visual design and the underlying data, a demand that often exceeds the capabilities of non-experts. To address this, we conducted a crowdsourcing study involving 1,000 participants tasked with analyzing various information visualizations. We gathered their interpretations, recorded their self-reported proficiency, and captured their screen interactions. Our analysis of these elements revealed that sample data points significantly aid comprehension for those with lower skill levels. Consequently, we propose a design strategy for novices that involves incorporating representative samples within visualizations.

Lieb's theorem establishes that for a system of $N$ bosons occupying a single-particle Hilbert space, the ground state energy of a non-interacting Hamiltonian is uniquely defined by a specific density matrix. This paper demonstrates that this unique state is a pure state, and we explore the physical implications of this finding. Furthermore, we examine the entropy of the condensate fraction resulting from ground state projections onto various pure states. Our analysis reveals a striking phenomenon: the condensate fraction exhibits a peak for a specific pure state, and we investigate the characteristics of this state.

Counterfactual reasoning is essential for understanding the impact of specific actions, yet it remains difficult to implement in practice. This paper addresses scenarios where an agent possesses sufficient information to determine whether a desired outcome would have occurred under a specific action, but lacks the necessary data to evaluate this possibility under different conditions. The objective is to identify a strategy that maximizes the probability of achieving a desired result, even when faced with uncertainty about the success of alternative strategies. The proposed approach involves selecting a strategy that minimizes the distributional uncertainty surrounding its success probability. The study demonstrates that this uncertainty can be effectively quantified using a metric derived from the Fisher information matrix. The analysis reveals that this matrix is highly sensitive to the specific parameterization of the underlying distribution. Consequently, the work introduces a novel parameterization that yields a strategy with reduced distributional uncertainty. The authors further prove that this new parameterization is optimal in the sense that it results in the lowest possible variance for the estimated success probability. The paper concludes by providing a numerical example that illustrates the practical benefits of this approach.

Urban noise categorization is a critical task for environmental monitoring, traffic analysis, and the creation of soundscapes. While recent studies have introduced various methods for this purpose, they often rely on different datasets, making fair comparisons between approaches impossible. To address this, we present a unified dataset for urban noise categorization alongside a robust baseline model. We also establish a rigorous protocol for evaluating and comparing methods. Our results indicate that the proposed baseline achieves an accuracy of 70.3% on the test set.

We examine the general framework for constructing global symmetry-breaking terms within the context of Type IIB effective field theories (EFTs). Our analysis reveals that these symmetry-breaking terms can be broadened to include extensions of the standard theta-term, which manifest as axionic couplings to the field strengths of any $T$-invariant gauge fields. We demonstrate that the axionic component of such extended theta-terms is constrained by the same geometric and topological conditions governing the pure theta-term itself. Furthermore, we establish that the symmetry-breaking nature of these extended theta-term modifications is governed by a generalized version of the D-term theorem.

This work introduces an algorithm designed to learn Nash equilibria in stochastic, turn-based, two-player, zero-sum games. Departing from traditional methods that rely on value iteration, our approach employs a randomized algorithm that identifies a compact set of strategies for one player, enabling them to achieve the maximum possible game value against any strategy from the opposing entity. The algorithm's convergence is demonstrated through a randomized process that repeatedly refines the player's strategy set. The proposed method is evaluated across two scenarios: a classic game and a simulation-driven game featuring a complex reward function. The results indicate that the algorithm can effectively learn equilibria in both environments.

This work presents a logic for reasoning about Aristotle's modal syllogism, a system that integrates traditional Aristotelian logic with modal elements derived from European scholasticism. By defining the system as a three-valued framework, we establish a sound and complete proof calculus and define its semantics through possible-worlds models.

Causal relationships are vital for comprehending quantum phenomena, and the causal structure within quantum circuits is typically determined by the sequential ordering of gates. This study demonstrates that gate ordering alone is insufficient to define quantum causality; rather, the causal architecture can vary significantly depending on the measurement basis and the specific detection strategy employed. We illustrate this counterintuitive result by showing that the causal framework of a quantum circuit can diverge from its mathematical representation as a directed acyclic graph. Furthermore, we reveal that this discrepancy arises because quantum nodes can function as both causes and effects, contingent upon the chosen detection method.

This study introduces a frame-level dual-critic reinforcement learning (RL) architecture designed for bit allocation in High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC). The proposed method employs a dual-critic framework to address the inherent trade-off between the immediate cost associated with quantization parameters (QPs) and the predictive quality of the reconstructed video frames. The first critic, termed the Q-value network, estimates the total quantization cost, while the second critic, the V-value network, forecasts the future video distortion. By synthesizing outputs from both networks, the system determines the optimal QP for each frame. Experimental findings indicate that this approach outperforms existing methods, particularly in scenarios with limited training data, and effectively balances quantization costs against video distortion.

We investigate the chemical evolution of protoplanetary disks, specifically focusing on the transition from carbon-rich to oxygen-rich environments. Our findings indicate that the destruction of carbon-resistant grains in the outer disk regions triggers a chemical shift toward an oxygen-rich composition. This destruction process is driven by the combined effects of cosmic-ray irradiation and UV exposure, which cause carbonaceous grains to sublimate. Consequently, the release of carbon into the gas phase facilitates the formation of CO, thereby depleting the available oxygen in solid form and promoting the conversion of oxygen-bearing ices into gaseous CO. This mechanism is particularly significant in disks with low masses, where the transition to an oxygen-rich chemistry can occur at large distances, extending up to 100 astronomical units.

Cutting plane (CP) methods are highly effective for solving mixed-integer programs (MIPs) and are extensively utilized in industry. However, the efficiency of these methods is heavily dependent on the quality of dynamically generated cuts. This paper introduces a novel machine learning framework designed to select optimal cutting planes during MIP resolution. The core of this approach is a new algorithm that iterates through CP subproblems and employs supervised learning to predict the most beneficial cuts for each stage. By using a look-ahead strategy, the method evaluates the impact of every candidate cut on the subproblem's resolution time, prioritizing those with the most significant effects. The selection of high-quality training data is achieved by integrating a heuristic search with the look-ahead mechanism. The system is further strengthened through imitation learning, which fine-tunes the selection policy based on the heuristic-generated data. Experimental results on a substantial set of benchmark MIP instances demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Weyl semimetals are characterized by the presence of Weyl nodes, which act as sources or sinks for Berry curvature in momentum space. These nodes are typically protected by inversion symmetry and time-reversal symmetry, though they can also be generated by the breaking of one of these symmetries. This study reports on Weyl semimetal properties in iridium-doped MoTe$_{2}$ (Mo$_{0.9}$Ir$_{0.1}$Te$_{2}$), a system where inversion symmetry is disrupted. Transport measurements reveal a superconducting transition at $T_c = 3.7$ K. The normal-state resistivity follows a linear temperature dependence ($\rho \propto T$), a behavior characteristic of Dirac fermions. Furthermore, the specific heat data indicates a linear temperature coefficient ($\gamma$), signifying a metallic electronic state with a density of states at the Fermi level. These findings suggest that the observed superconductivity in Mo$_{0.9}$Ir$_{0.1}$Te$_{2}$ arises from Cooper pairing of Dirac fermions within a Weyl semimetal context.

Software development relies on bug reporting as a vital tool for managing defects, with product managers utilizing these reports to prioritize and resolve issues. However, the sheer volume of submitted reports makes it difficult for developers to identify critical bugs, leading to inefficient prioritization and resolution processes. To address this challenge, we introduce an automated tagging system that leverages natural language understanding to extract key characteristics from bug reports. By applying a state-of-the-art language model to this task, we achieved a 0.63 F1-score, outperforming existing solutions.

This study examines the electronic structure of nonisotropic graphene, specifically analyzing the impact of a tilted Fermi level on its electronic phase diagram. We demonstrate that within a nonisotropic regime, the grapheme undergoes transitions between Dirac semimetal, Weyl semimetal, and Chern insulator phases. Furthermore, we investigate the interplay between symmetry breaking and phase transitions, revealing that transitions between the Dirac semimetal and Chern insulator phases are second-order, whereas transitions between the Dirac semimetal and Weyl semimetal phases are first-order.

This study introduces a new approach to remotely supervised named entity recognition (NER) that utilizes an instructor learning model to generate candidate entity mentions and a student ensemble method to validate them. The system architecture employs a dedicated NER model for student classification, while the instructor learns to predict link types between entity mentions and possible entities via a custom algorithm. The resulting student ensemble is refined by addressing the class imbalance inherent in training data and mitigating the impact of unreliable predictions from the instructor-based ensemble. Extensive experiments on the CoNLL-2003 dataset demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art performance, with results significantly exceeding those of previous methods.

Social media has become a vital tool for gathering user-generated content, offering a cost-effective and efficient method for gathering data compared to traditional methods. This study examines the application of text mining techniques to extract insights regarding tourist experiences from social media platforms, specifically focusing on Twitter. By analyzing tweets related to the city of Xi'an, China, we demonstrate how unstructured textual data can be transformed into structured information to support decision-making. The paper outlines a comprehensive methodology for data collection, including the creation of a thesaurus, data cleaning, and the construction of a knowledge base. Furthermore, we detail the process of mining Twitter data to generate a knowledge graph, which serves as a foundation for developing a decision support system. This system enables the visualization of tourist experiences through a knowledge map, facilitating the analysis of experience quality and the identification of areas requiring improvement. Ultimately, this approach provides a robust framework for leveraging social media data to enhance decision-making within the tourism sector.

The paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing material microstructures, utilizing a method to calculate the information content inherent in their mechanical responses. This approach is founded on the concept of a material's internal architecture being encoded within its behavior, which can be deciphered by examining the relationship between distinct mechanical characteristics. By applying this methodology to synthetic microstructures, the study successfully reconstructs hidden features from the material's microstructure using only measurable mechanical properties. This demonstrates that the proposed method offers a robust means to interpret the connection between microstructural design and observable mechanical performance.

We introduce a novel potential that reveals a unique physical phenomenon: charged particles following approximately circular paths with centers located away from the potential's minimum. Accurately estimating the paths of multiple objects is vital for applications like autonomous driving and air traffic management. While existing methods often rely on forward simulation, they suffer from two main limitations: they cannot account for unobserved objects, and they frequently fail to capture the full range of potential trajectories. To overcome these issues, we introduce a novel backward simulation approach that incorporates both seen and unseen objects. This method begins by generating a set of possible end positions for each target, then iteratively simulates their origins based on these end points. By applying a filtering step to eliminate implausible paths at each iteration, we ensure only feasible trajectories remain. Finally, we validate this approach using a realistic traffic scenario, demonstrating its effectiveness.

This paper introduces a new multi-infeed stability assessment framework for AC grids containing Voltage Source Converters (VSCs) that utilize an admittance-based matrix representation. The resulting model is converted into a system of linear equations, from which a characteristic equation is derived to formulate stability criteria. These criteria are expressed through a collection of complex coefficients within a polynomial, enabling the application of the Routh-Hurwitz criterion to derive stability conditions. Furthermore, the method is applied to a two-infeed scenario to illustrate the impact of inter-converter interactions on stability. The findings indicate that the proposed method offers superior accuracy compared to existing admittance matrix techniques, as it explicitly includes the VSC equivalent impedance model.

This study examines the intrinsic complexity and repeatability of online signature dynamics. This study investigates the problem of estimating $Y$ based on observed $X$ using Bregman divergence as a measure of disparity between inferential methods. We establish consistency and an asymptotic normal distribution for minimum Bregman-based inference, demonstrating that these findings hold broadly across a wide range of Bregman diversifics, not just specific ones. Furthermore, we prove that minimum Bregman $q$-divergence estimation is both consistent and asymptotically normal even when dealing with zero cells in contingency tables. We also extend these findings to include cases involving missing data.

This study introduces a novel approach to view synthesis for dynamic scenes, enabling the generation of novel views from sparse, unconstrained monocular sequences. We propose a method that simultaneously estimates geometry and appearance by leveraging a novel cross-frame cross-view interaction mechanism. This mechanism effectively captures both inter-frame and inter-view dependencies, allowing the system to reconstruct geometry and appearance by synthesizing information across multiple temporal and spatial perspectives. We further demonstrate that this interaction mechanism can be integrated with various existing neural rendering architectures. Experimental results indicate that our approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in view synthesis for both unconstrained sequences and those with sparse sampling.

This study introduces a boundary-agnostic spectral statistic, termed the mean spectral distance, which offers a method for linking the energy spectra of quantum graphs to their classical analogs without relying on semiclassical limits. This approach is applicable to both open and closed quantum graphs, including those with boundaries. The core methodology involves calculating the mean spectral distance between a quantum graph's spectrum and that of a reference spectrum derived from a classical graph. This reference spectrum is constructed by applying the Fourier transform to the trace of the resolvent for the classical operator, specifically utilizing a spectral density function that is independent of boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the variation in mean spectral distance across different graphs can be linked to specific geometric and topological characteristics of the underlying classical graph. Furthermore, we illustrate that the mean spectral distance remains invariant for classical graphs that are topologically equivalent, even when the specific quantum boundary conditions differ.

This paper introduces a new method for determining the periods of periodic variable stars. The technique involves plotting the time series data as a function of time against a specific phase, which generates a phase-folded light curve. By analyzing the peak and valley points of this phase-folded curve, the method calculates the amplitude and the amplitude's derivative for every sample point. These metrics are utilized to construct a specific function, which is then integrated to produce a normalized curve. A correlation coefficient is subsequently computed between this normalized curve and the phase-folded light curve to determine the period. The authors have validated this approach using both simulated and real-world data, demonstrating its effectiveness.

A framework qualifies as "near-ideal" if it can be transformed into an ideal one through small adjustments. This property is crucial for near-ideal controller design, a method that leverages insights derived from an ideal system to create a controller for a system that is only approximately ideal. This paper addresses the challenge of identifying the closest Negative Imaginary (NI) framework to a given one. We demonstrate that for a general framework, determining this nearest Near-Ideal NI (NI) class framework is NP-hard. Conversely, we prove that when dealing with linear frameworks, the problem of finding the nearest ideal NI framework is solvable in polynomial time. Additionally, we establish that finding the closest Linear Fractional (LFI) framework to a general linear framework is NP-hard, though a polynomial-time solution exists for finding the nearest LFI that is also linear. These findings are applied to the problem of near-ideal controller design.

This paper presents a novel method for continuously training end-to-end speech recognition systems. Our approach involves a teacher-student framework where a teacher model processes mini-batches of data, and the resulting transcriptions are used to train a student model. The student model then feeds back its own predictions to the teacher, enabling a continuous learning process. We demonstrate that this ongoing training strategy effectively prevents performance degradation caused by catastrophic interference.

Code-switching refers to the practice of alternating between two or more languages within a single utterance. While numerous code-switching datasets exist, most focus on sociolinguistic aspects, leaving gaps in emotional analysis. To address this, we introduce a new Code-Switching Emotion Dataset (CSED) featuring 1,000 manually annotated utterances in a code-switched variety of English and Spanish. Alongside this new resource, we present the results of our experiments on emotion classification across multiple multilingual datasets, employing various deep learning models.

This study examines a minimal three-loop radiative seesaw framework that simultaneously incorporates a mechanism for small-scale type-I seesaw, generates baryon asymmetry via thermal type-III leptogenesis, and offers a dark matter candidate. We demonstrate that the model can account for observed small-scale leptonic matter through thermal production of right-handed neutrinos, which subsequently decay to create the requisite baryon asymmetry. Furthermore, the model yields a viable explanation for dark energy by introducing a non-minimal coupling between the Higgs field and the Ricci scalar. We also derive the model's predictions for the relic abundance of dark matter, the neutrino mass spectrum, and the effective neutrino number ($N_{\rm eff}$).

Neural networks have recently demonstrated significant success in predicting human reactions. This study introduces a novel item-based neural network architecture designed to forecast individual reactions to specific items. The model incorporates a mechanism to account for sequential user-item interactions, which are critical for anticipating responses in dynamic environments. Experimental results indicate that this approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in terms of performance.

This study introduces a novel robust collaborative design for an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) within a cell-free network (CFN) environment. By leveraging the low-rank characteristics of the channel matrix, the proposed framework jointly optimizes the transmit beamforming vectors at access points (APs) and the phase shifts of the IRS. To address potential channel estimation errors, the problem is formulated as a robust optimization task involving uncertainty sets. To solve this, a hybrid approach combining the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) with a successive convex approximation (SCA) algorithm is developed. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms benchmark solutions in terms of sum-rate performance.

This study introduces a new approach to dynamic branch forecasting, a technique designed to estimate future customer counts at a specific location by integrating historical data with real-time observations. We propose a deep learning framework that utilizes recurrent neural networks to model the temporal dependencies between past and real-time data, thereby generating forecasts for various horizons. We assess the performance of this method against current state-of-the-art solutions, including traditional time-series models and existing deep learning architectures. Empirical results indicate that our model achieves superior accuracy compared to its competitors. Furthermore, we examine the interpretability of our model by analyzing its learned representations and weight matrices to gain insights into forecast generation. Finally, we discuss the practical applications of dynamic branch forecasting within the retail sector, highlighting its potential to enhance operational efficiency and customer experiences.

This study introduces a novel active camera management system designed to detect objects using deep learning. Drawing inspiration from mimicry, the proposed approach utilizes a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to analyze both color and texture cues, enabling the camera to dynamically adjust its orientation toward the target. Specifically, the system calculates the probability of the object being located within the current field of view (FOV) and directs the camera incrementally to ensure the object remains centered. Experimental results indicate that this method surpasses existing solutions in both speed and accuracy. Furthermore, the study examines how texture and color characteristics influence the detection of camouflaged objects.

This article focuses on the Gibbs measure of a specific Ising model on the two-dimensional integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$, where the interaction strength between adjacent spins is modulated by the sum of their coordinates. The associated Gibbs measure exhibits a phase transition at a critical temperature $T_c$. We also prove that there exists a specific temperature $T_1$, situated strictly between $T_1 < T_c$, where a unique translation-invariant solution to this disparity equation exists.

We investigate the dynamical behavior of two V-type atoms interacting with a structured reservoir, where each atom possesses two excited states and one ground state. Our analysis reveals that the atom-light interaction is highly sensitive to the specific configuration of the excited states. We demonstrate that a stationary subradiant state can be achieved when one excited state is shared between the atoms, provided they interact with a structured environment that suppresses transitions to the other excited state. Conversely, a steady-state superspin state emerges when shared states are avoided, enabled by a resonant reservoir that drives superradiant transitions. These findings offer a refined understanding of the mechanisms governing light-matter interactions in multi-level atomic systems.

This study examines the asymptotic stability of a kink exhibiting internal oscillations within the sine-Gordon (SG) equation, subject to a localized disturbance with a small, constant odd amplitude. We demonstrate that a sufficiently small perturbation results in the kink's asymptotic stability. Furthermore, we establish that the kink's final oscillation frequency converges to the internal oscillation frequency of the kink at rest.

The J-PARC facility, situated in Tokai, Japan, is scheduled to commence operations in 2015. It is designed to deliver high-intensity beams of protons, pions, and kaons, enabling comprehensive investigations into hadron science. A primary objective of the J-HADES experiment is to investigate the phenomenon of color transparency, which involves the reduced interaction of hadrons with their target medium. This study aims to achieve two goals: first, to determine the interaction cross-section of hadrons with reduced quantum fluctuations, and second, to utilize color transparency as a probe for the nuclear medium. The experimental strategy involves analyzing the momentum transfer within the nucleus and the resulting increase in hadron escape probability.

Consistency training is a powerful technique for enhancing the robustness of neural networks against adversarial attacks. This paper introduces a novel method for consistency training that is specifically designed to address scenarios where the input data is discrete, such as images with a limited palette. Our approach involves training the network to maintain consistency in the output despite the perturbation of the input data by a "virtual adversary." We evaluate this method on a classification task using a discrete dataset, specifically the MNIST handwritten digits dataset. Our results demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to existing approaches in terms of consistency training.

Endoscopy is a minimally invasive procedure used to diagnose colorectal polyps, which are often precancerous. While deep learning has shown great promise for detecting these polyps, most existing methods focus on single-frame analysis, neglecting the temporal dynamics inherent in endoscopic videos. To address this, we introduce a multi-frame cooperative framework that integrates information across multiple frames. The approach begins by employing a spatio-temporal feature transformation to capture time-aware representations from various frames. Subsequently, we utilize a multi-frame cooperative module to enhance the model's ability to utilize cross-frame data. This module employs a cross-frame attention mechanism to weigh the significance of different frames and a cross-frame fusion module to aggregate features effectively. Extensive experiments on the Kvasir-Colon dataset demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art single-frame detectors, achieving a 2.1% increase in mIoU and a 10.1% increase in mAP. Furthermore, we address the computational cost of our approach by implementing a multi-frame sampling strategy, which reduces the FLOPs by 30% while maintaining comparable performance. The source code is available at https://github.com/Chenrui1995/MultiCo.

This paper introduces a new algorithm designed for sampling from stream populations that features an unequal chance of selection for each element. The algorithm assigns a specific sampling probability based on the index of each stream element, and our primary contribution is the derivation of a closed-form formula for this probability.

This study examines reaction-diffusion equations featuring nonlocal boundary conditions on uneven domains. It demonstrates that the asymptotic behavior of nonlocal reaction-diffusion systems can be effectively modeled by an extended system on a uniform domain through appropriate reflection of the domain. This approach involves symmetric extension of the solution to handle the nonlocal boundary constraints.

Ultra-Compact Dwarfs (UCDs) are massive, dense stellar systems that are believed to be stripped cores of dwarf galaxies. While UCDs are typically found in the nearby universe, the authors have developed a machine learning (ML) framework to identify them in the deep universe. This study utilizes the Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS) to train a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) capable of identifying UCDs. To enhance interpretability, the authors employed Grad-CAM, an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) method, to analyze the CNN's decision-making process. The Grad-CAM results revealed that the model primarily relies on the presence of point sources and the detection of red giant stars. Furthermore, the authors propose a novel classification scheme for UCDs, categorizing them into three distinct groups: UCDs, Globular Group UCDs (GGUCDs), and Globular Groups (GGS). GGUCDs are defined as systems with masses between $10^5$ and $10^6$ solar masses, while GGS represent objects with masses below $10^5$ solar masses. The study concludes that the proposed ML approach offers a robust method for identifying extragalactic UCDs and GGUs, with the added benefit of enabling the classification of globular groups.

Recommendation systems are essential to the digital economy, serving as a primary driver of revenue for online platforms. Consequently, there is a competitive drive among businesses to refine these systems, which has led to a surge in research and development. However, the inherent complexity of these systems often makes rigorous evaluation challenging. This paper examines the utility of simulations in suggesting recommendation frameworks, reviewing current literature on this topic, and outlining the specific obstacles encountered when implementing simulations within a commercial setting.

This study investigates the hypothesis testing of sample means under conditions of extremely heavy tails. We specifically examine the scenario where the population variance is undefined, utilizing a truncated sample average to construct test statistics. Our findings demonstrate that this test statistic converges asymptotically to a normal distribution. Furthermore, we evaluate the test's power and conduct an empirical comparison with the traditional t-test.

This study introduces a novel Sinc-convolutional neural network (CNN) framework designed to address the classification of motor visual imagery in EEG-based brain-computer interfaces (CBIs). The proposed method leverages Sinc-convolutional layers to automatically extract spatial features from raw EEG signals, eliminating the need for traditional bandpass filtering, spatial feature extraction, and channel selection. Additionally, we developed a new EEG-based motor visualization classification technique utilizing a deep neural network (DNN) that integrates the aforementioned Sinc-CNN with a fully connected DNN. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed Sinc-CNN-DNN architecture outperforms both the individual Sinc-CNN and a standard deep learning baseline. Specifically, it achieves an average classification accuracy of 74.7% and a balanced accuracy of 74.2% across all subjects.

We examine the relationship between the principle of noncommutative geometry and the principle of relativity within the framework of noncommutative $AdS_2$. Our analysis reveals that the latter decomposes into two distinct components: first, the principle of noncommutative Lorentz transformations, which is governed by noncommutative geometry and remains invariant under noncommutative Lorentz boosts; and second, the principle of noncommutative relativity (governing the dynamics of particles and fields), which is independent of noncommutative geometry.

This study examines the concept of ideal matching within the realm of incompatible kidney exchanges, utilizing a real-world dataset from the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) to analyze actual operational practices. We introduce a new Ideal Acceptance problem that incorporates constraints on both the recipient and the donor-provided organ, noting that this formulation is computationally NP-hard. To address this challenge, we present a framework based on bipartite graph theory and develop a corresponding algorithm. This approach is then evaluated against current industry standards through computational experiments. Our findings indicate that the proposed method offers a more robust strategy for ideal matching compared to existing methods.

This study introduces a hybrid Markov-LSTM model designed to enhance the capabilities of both LSTM and Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). The proposed framework utilizes HMMs to generate state sequences, which subsequently serve as inputs for an LSTM network to predict the final output. By integrating these approaches, the model leverages the strengths of each to achieve superior performance. Experimental results indicate that this hybridization strategy yields improved accuracy and efficiency compared to using either the LSTM or HMM independently.

This paper investigates the boundedness and compactness properties of generalized Toeplitz operators acting on weighted Bergman spaces over bounded strongly pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb{C}^n$. Furthermore, we establish boundedness criteria for generalized Volterra operators on weighted Bergman spaces associated with the same domains.

In this paper, we present a model compression strategy designed to optimize cross-lingual multi-job models for low-resource languages. The primary objective is to minimize the computational cost of translation while maintaining high performance. We achieve this by training a single, unified model capable of handling multiple languages, which utilizes a shared embedding space for translation tasks. This architecture incorporates a dedicated cross-lingual attention mechanism to effectively capture relationships between linguistic pairs. Furthermore, we introduce a novel job-specific attention layer that enhances the model's ability to process diverse tasks. We also evaluate various model compression techniques, including quantization and pruning, to reduce the model's size. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach yields an average relative improvement of 1.5% in F1 scores compared to baseline models, while achieving a 4.2x reduction in model size.

In the realm of data science, the phrase "data is the new oil" is widely recognized, yet it is frequently misunderstood. Although oil is typically extracted and refined before distribution, data often remains in its raw form, leading to confusion regarding the optimal timing, location, and method for data sharing. This perspective argues that sharing data in its original state is rarely the best approach, drawing a parallel to how oil undergoes processing to become a more effective end product. Consequently, the argument suggests that data should similarly be refined to unlock its full potential. This refinement can occur at various stages, from the initial data collection phase to the final deployment stage.

This paper investigates decomposed maps from Jacobian varieties of hyperelliptic curves to those arising from algebraic curves with lower genus. Drawing upon an earlier finding by Howe regarding the uniqueness of such mappings for genus 2 and 3 cases, the authors generalize this result to genus 2 and 3 decomposed richelot mappings. Additionally, they introduce a family of curves termed "generalized Howe curves" which possess the characteristic of possessing a unique polarized isogeny to the product of elliptic curves and the Jacobian of a genus 2 curve.

We address the challenge of estimating a $d \times d$ symmetric, positive semi-definite (PSD) matrix $\Theta$ with a rank of at most $k$, under the assumption that the data consists of $n$ independent samples from a multivariate Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, \Theta)$. We introduce a novel method named Gaussian Reduction (GR) that leverages the fact that the eigenvalues of $\Theta$ are non-increasing. This approach involves sequentially subtracting rank-1 PSD matrices from $\Theta$ to reduce its rank to $k$. We demonstrate that the resulting estimator, $\hat{\Theta}_{GR}$, is both unbiased and positive semi-definite. Furthermore, we establish that $\hat{\Theta}_{GR}$ achieves an optimal minimax rate of convergence for this specific low-rank PSD matrix estimation problem. We also prove that $\hat{\Theta}_{GR}$ is a volume-optimal estimator, meaning it minimizes the determinant of the asymptotic covariance matrix of the Gaussian maximum likelihood estimator for $\Theta$. Finally, we validate the efficacy of this estimator through numerical experiments.

Wikipedia stands as a premier example of the Web 2.0 phenomenon, where user-generated content is a defining feature. As a collaborative project, its articles are constructed through the combined efforts of numerous users, with every modification recorded in the page revision history. This mechanism allows researchers to analyze the evolution of articles over time, a capability that has been extensively utilized in studies of collaboration, social networks, and the dynamics of knowledge creation. However, this raw revision data is typically available only in verbose DiffML format, which complicates its integration with other Web 2.0 resources. To address this, the authors introduce WikiHist.html, an initiative designed to export Wikipedia's complete revision logs into a human-readable HTML structure. This format facilitates the seamless incorporation of edit data into Web 2.0 frameworks, enabling the development of user-friendly interfaces for browsing and analyzing article changes.

We introduce a polar meron-antimeron grid characterized by a twisted bilayer structure, where each meron and antimeron functions as a topological defect within a single twisted layer. This configuration is feasible in systems exhibiting a non-coplanar order parameter, such as those with complex order parameters like the chiral $A$-phase superfluid or a specific type of magnet. Within these systems, the polar nature of the lattice arises from the radial orientation of the order at each defect. We demonstrate that this arrangement is energetically favored in the presence of an external magnetic field, which is capable of inducing the necessary non-coplanar order. Furthermore, we explore the potential for creating and manipulating these structures using vortices in the superfluid order.

This study explores the concept of "existence" within the framework of General Relativity, utilizing the language of differential geometry. It establishes that the concept of "being present" in spacetime is formalized through the requirement that the tangent bundle, defined over a manifold, must admit a connection. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the presence of such a connection corresponds to the existence of the vertical endomorphism on the tangent bundle. Finally, the authors derive the equivalent conditions for this vertical endomorphism to be an integrable geometric structure.

We introduce a new method to create controllable, tunable channels within nematic liquid crystals (NLCs) by utilizing a planar surface subjected to sinusoidal deformations. This patterned substrate generates an analogous undulating texture in the NLC, the bulk of which reorients into a uniform state. When placed between a second planar surface, the resulting NLC cell exhibits a distinct phase transition: as the NLC aligns to match the substrate, the emerging phase is defined by the geometry of these surface-induced undulations. Consequently, these arrangements generate effective potential wells that trap colloidal particles. Furthermore, by adjusting the sinusoidal parameters, the resulting pathways can be fine-tuned to specific dimensions, allowing the generation of particle traps with adjustable depths and widths.

This study examines how an asteroid's shape affects its vulnerability to external forces during a distant encounter with a planet. We introduce a new approach that models the asteroid as a collection of discrete particles, allowing us to calculate the dynamical stability of the resulting debris field. By analyzing the dynamical evolution of the system, we determine the sensitivity of the asteroid's exterior to these external forces. Our findings indicate that the asteroid's form plays a critical role in debris ejection, with elongated asteroids exhibiting a significantly higher sensitivity to external forces compared to spherical asteroids. These findings are particularly relevant for understanding the asteroid's response during close planetary passages and offer valuable insights for the design of asteroid deflection missions.

We introduce a quantum algorithm designed to sample rare conformations within a molecular system, utilizing quantum simulation of the corresponding Hamiltonian. This approach offers exponential speedups over classical methods for sampling rare events, contingent on the feasibility of executing quantum state tomography. We examine the algorithm's efficacy in sampling the transition of a single peptide from one structural state to another, alongside a comparison of this technique with classical methods for sampling rare events.

Polarization measurements of the inverse-Compton scattered light from relativistic jets offer a novel method to probe the magnetic field structure within jets. This approach is particularly valuable for studying the jet origins of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), where the scattering geometry is well-defined, allowing for a direct inference of the magnetic field's orientation at the emission site. This study introduces MAPPIES, a Monte-Carlo simulation designed to model the polarization of inverse-Compton radiation generated by relativistic electrons interacting with blackbody photons. The code incorporates a comprehensive set of physical processes, including synchrotron emission, Compton scattering, synchrotron self-Compton emission, and pair production. We present the simulation's initial validation and demonstrate its application to GRB jets, yielding a predicted polarization degree of 10% for the scattered light. This value aligns with recent observational data from the GRB 190829A afterglow, which recorded a polarization of 12% at 1.4 GHz.

This study presents a novel approach to modeling Arctic sea ice thickness, diverging from traditional methods that rely on fixed grid-point height maps. Instead, we define the ice thickness distribution as a probability density function (PDF) of thickness values, which we track continuously over time. This PDF is derived from satellite-derived column area distributions, which are then fitted using a selected parametric family. Our results indicate that a two-parameter Gamma PDF provides the most accurate representation of the data. To simulate the evolution of this distribution, we employ a simplified thermodynamic thickness evolution equation, which is then discretized into a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). This discretization is achieved through a probabilistic method that incorporates stochastic forcing to account for uncertain heat fluxes. Furthermore, we introduce a new analytical solution to the ODE describing the ice thickness distribution, which is validated against numerical simulations. Finally, we demonstrate that this analytical solution can effectively reproduce the seasonal cycle of Arctic sea ice thickness.

This paper introduces and investigates the concept of the generalized Weierstrass semigroup at multiple points on specific maximal curves. We determine this semigroup for the $X$ curve at multiple points under two scenarios: when $k=4$ with $n=2$, and when $k=6$ with $n=2$. Additionally, we handle the case where $k=5$ and $n=1$. These findings extend previously known results regarding the semigroup at single points on the Hermitian curve.

Deep learning-based singing voice generation (SVG) has garnered significant interest from both researchers and practitioners. This survey offers a comprehensive overview of existing SVG architectures, examining their underlying principles, primary objectives, and key findings. The authors critically analyze prevalent evaluation metrics and associated challenges, while also highlighting promising future research avenues.

To address this, we introduce the NIPS4Bplus dataset, which includes 1,000 recordings from 100 species across 100 distinct species. Event cameras are emerging as a promising technology for robotics and computer vision, yet their raw data is inherently challenging to interpret. This difficulty stems from the asynchronous nature of the sensor, which produces a stream of individual events, and the lack of a defined relationship between an event's intensity and its reported amplitude. This paper introduces a method to rectify event camera data, transforming it into a format compatible with existing vision algorithms. The proposed approach involves a calibration step to determine the relationship between event intensity and amplitude, followed by an optimization process to align event data with a specific imaging model. We evaluate this method using both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness through various visual tasks.

Graphs serve as a versatile data structure capable of representing diverse real-world scenarios, including social networks, knowledge graphs, graphs, and molecular structures. Consequently, graph-based learning has become a rapidly expanding field within machine learning. This review paper examines the fundamental principles of graphs, outlines their primary applications, and critically analyzes existing graph learning methodologies. Furthermore, it highlights unsolved challenges and suggests potential directions for future research.

We present a full set of full subcategory definitions for the algebraic K-theory spectra of $\Sigma _{ 2 }$, which fills in gaps left in previous studies by Bhatt, Langer, and Zink. Our approach involves a novel method for constructing the logarithmic structure on the scheme $\Sigma _{ 2 }$, which is then utilized to generate these collections. Additionally, we offer an alternative derivation of the logarithmic structure that aligns with the method proposed by Kato.

This study introduces a beacon-driven 3D directional system designed for retinal surgery, specifically addressing the critical need to guide the surgeon's tool orientation during vitreoretinal procedures. The system utilizes a beacon mounted on the surgical instrument to track its 3D position via a camera system comprising two infrared emitters and two cameras. By leveraging beacon information, the system calculates the tool's 3D direction in real-time and displays this guidance on an augmented reality interface to support the surgeon. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a positional accuracy of 1.5 mm and an angular accuracy of 10.8°, indicating strong potential for clinical application in retinal surgery.

The paper focuses on studying quadratic Gaussian F- polynomials. Two distinct recurrence relations for these polynomials are presented, alongside a full analysis of their numerical behavior in terms of real and imaginary components.

The advent of Apple's Watch and Facepod devices, coupled with Apple Watch, has sparked a new wave of research into biometric authentication. This technology is now integrated into Apple Watch, Apple Watch, and other devices, including the latest iPhone models. Google and other tech giants have also introduced their own biometric authentication systems. This paper provides an overview of biometric authentication, focusing on the latest research and developments in this field. It also explores the potential applications and limitations of biometric authentication, as well as how it can be used to enhance security and privacy.

This study examines the Weyl-Wigner approach within the context of quantum lattice models, specifically focusing on how phase-space distributions are defined for these systems. We demonstrate that the corresponding Wigner functions are not merely uniform across all lattice sites but are inherently linked to the spatial Fourier transform of the system's density matrix. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of these functions in the continuum limit, showing that they converge to the standard Weyl-Wigner formulation applicable to continuous systems.

This study examines the impact of YouTube's interface design on user agency. We conducted a user study with 100 participants, presenting them with three distinct YouTube layouts: a desktop version, a mobile version, and an idealized, unrestricted interface. Participants were tasked with curating a personalized video playlist. Our findings indicate that users navigating through playlists on the mobile interface experienced the lowest levels of agency. Conversely, those using the desktop interface reported the highest sense of agency. This suggests that the specific arrangement of options and controls within a user interface significantly shapes the extent to which individuals feel capable of exercising agency.

This study demonstrates that the name-free (or pure) $\pi$-calculus possesses two significant properties: functional completeness and, for a specific fragment, finite executability. The latter implies that any function computable via the $\pi$-calculus admits a representation as an infinite tree of $\pi$-terms with a finite set of subterms. The proof relies on establishing an equational theory for the name-free $\pi$-calculus, a result that also yields the theorem of equational decidability for the name-free setting, a question previously unresolved. Furthermore, we present a theorem-schema establishing the finite executability of the $\pi$-calculus for the fragment defined by the absence of variable name bindings and limited parallel composition.
This paper introduces a method to generate a compacted Gray code based on the structural tree of a sequence.

The sPHENIX experiment, designed to operate within the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) at Brookhaven National Lab, aims to investigate the properties of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP). To achieve this, it relies on a hybrid detector system that combines a central tracking apparatus with a forward calorimeter. This paper details the implementation of a track-fitting algorithm tailored for the sPHENIX central tracking structure. By utilizing a Kalman filter, the method identifies tracks within dense particle environments, specifically those with transverse momenta exceeding 1 GeV/c. The study evaluates the track-fitting algorithm's performance through the analysis of 2012 RHIP data from Au+Au collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 200 GeV.

This study examines the spatial-temporal finite element method (STFEM) for random partial differential equations (PDEs) employing random temporal interpolation. The work establishes a rigorous framework for the jump term inherent in STFEM and demonstrates its equivalence with second-order methods based on random temporal interpolation. A key contribution is the proposal of a novel approximation for this jump term, which aligns with an alternative random temporal discretization strategy. Furthermore, numerical experiments are presented to validate the accuracy of this proposed approach.

This paper examines the presence of directed cycles within signed mono-directed networks, which feature exclusively positive edges. We establish that the smallest integer $k$ such that the $k$-th power of the adjacency matrix contains no zero entries corresponds precisely to the length of the shortest directed cycle. Building on this, we propose a polynomial-time algorithm to identify the shortest directed cycle and provide a full characterization of the sets of all cycles for both simple and general cases. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the adjacency matrix of any such mono-directed graph possesses at least one positive eigenvalue.

The Modular Subset Total problem seeks a subset of integers that sums to a specific target value modulo a given number. While NP-complete in general, it admits a polynomial-time solution when the subset size is restricted to O(log n). We present a deterministic algorithm running in time $O(2^{0.34n + o(n)})$ for the unrestricted version, representing a substantial improvement over previous exponential methods.

This study presents a catalog of 1,000 M-dwarf flares identified by the All-Sky Automated Survey for Supernovae (ASAS-SN) between 2014 and 2019. These events were selected based on a brightness increase of at least 1.5 magnitudes, with a minimum duration of 10 minutes. The catalog details the coordinates, flare magnitude, peak flux, and duration for each occurrence. We also provide the stellar classification, spectral type, and distance for the host stars, along with their rotational periods and flare frequency distributions. The catalog includes the calculated flare energy and the derived flare frequency distribution for each host star.
