We introduce a three-dimensional Dirac semimetal characterized by a combination of linear and parabolic dispersion relations. This system is defined by a tunable parameter that interpolates between a parabolic dispersion with Dirac nodes and a parabolic dispersion featuring a Dirac cone. We analyze the phase diagram of this system, identifying a gapped Dirac semimetal phase that emerges when the parameter transitions the system from the linear to the purely cubic regime. Within this gapped phase, the energy gap remains constant regardless of momentum, and the dispersion evolves from parabolic to cubic. We further examine the low-energy behavior of the quasiparticles, demonstrating that the density of states scales quadratically with energy ($E^2$) for the parabolic limit and linearly with energy ($E$) for the cubic limit.

Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety defined over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$. We say $X$ is semi-stable if it is a $\mathbb{F}_q$-scheme of finite type that embeds into a smooth scheme over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ via the characteristic zero generic fiber. We also define $X$ as a "lazy curve" if it is a projective curve within $X$ that is not contained in any proper closed subvariety of $X$. The main result states that for a lazy curve $X$ over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, there exists a sequence of points $P_n$ on $X$ such that the sequence of Frobenius eigenvalues associated with $P_n$ converges to the eigenvalues of the Frobenius endomorphism acting on the first cohomology group of $X$. This result is a consequence of the fact that the eigenvalues of the Frobenius endomorphism acting on the first cohomology group of a semi-stable variety are bounded.

Gravitational physics has recently entered a new era of discovery, with the LIGO and Virgo collaborations having already detected over 90 binary black hole mergers. This paper investigates the observability of higher-order gravitational wave modes in these systems, a phenomenon predicted by General Relativity to arise from asymmetric charge distributions in the merging bodies. We analyze how third-generation detectors, such as the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer, will significantly enhance detection capabilities compared to current facilities. Our results indicate that while LIGO and Virgo have identified only a handful of higher-mode signals, future observatories will detect them with high frequency. We further examine the utility of these signals for determining source parameters and measuring the speed of gravity. Our findings suggest that Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer observations will yield precise measurements of the speed of gravity with uncertainties as low as 0.01 and 0.03, respectively.

The Gaia mission has identified numerous astrometric anomalies, some of which are attributed to the gravitational influence of unseen companions. This study examines the feasibility of characterizing such objects by utilizing partial astrometric data. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the astrometric signature of a massive body can be detected even when only a fraction of the induced wobble is observed. We establish that the likelihood of identifying such a signal depends on the orbital period, the mass of the companion, the orbital inclination, and the specific fraction of the orbit captured. Furthermore, we introduce a novel statistical method to quantify the detection probability of a mass given a partial astrometric signal. Applying this approach to the Gaia DR2 catalog, we identify 1,000 sources with partial astrometric signatures that exhibit a potential for hosting objects with masses exceeding 10 Jupiter masses ($M_{\rm J}$) within orbital periods shorter than 10 years.

The 0/1 Knapsack problem is a well-known combinatorial optimization challenge that has been widely addressed using Genetic Algorithms (GA). This study evaluates the performance of various selection and crossover methods in GAs by benchmarking them against each other. To achieve this, a novel framework was developed to assess the convergence of GA-based approaches for the 0/1 Knapsack problem. The analysis focuses on convergence speed and the quality of the final solutions. The results indicate that uniform selection and uniform crossover are the most effective techniques, whereas tournament selection and crossover exhibit superior performance.

Hatred speech detection is a critical task in natural language processing, yet existing methods often struggle with the scarcity of labeled data and the inherent subjectivity of the labels. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach that integrates three key techniques: (1) fine-tuning the T5 model, (2) enhanced data preparation, and (3) an ensemble learning strategy. Our experiments demonstrate that this ensemble model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Twitter Hate Speech Detection Challenge, reaching a macro F1 score of 0.834.

This study examines the scaling attributes of the Quantum Monte Carlo interaction for heavier ions, specifically focusing on $^{3}$He+$, $^{4}$He+, and $^{40}$Ar+. The results indicate that the interaction strength is proportional to the mass number ($A$) of the ion, with the proportionality constant remaining consistent across different elements. This finding aligns with prior research on hydrogen and deuterium, confirming a universal scaling behavior independent of the specific isotopes involved.

Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) are increasingly recognized as a robust approach for quantifying uncertainty in deep learning, yet their training is hindered by the high computational costs associated with exact Bayesian inference. This study introduces a novel method for training BNNs that employs a variational framework to approximate the posterior distribution. To address the inherent complexity of representing high-dimensional posteriors, we propose a new neural network architecture that embeds the parameters of a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) within its structure. This design enables the approximation of posterior distributions with arbitrary shapes and dimensions. Our approach is validated on both regression and classification tasks, demonstrating its efficacy.

Electron transfer (ET) in condensed matter systems is a foundational process in chemistry and biology, with Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory remaining a cornerstone for investigating ET in environments featuring vibrational modes. Despite its extensive utility, the theoretical underpinnings of this framework have been elusive. This work establishes a semiclassical instanton formulation for the rate constant within Marcus-Levich-Jortner theory, revealing that the ET rate is governed by a one-dimensional instanton trajectory. This approach offers a robust, intuitive, and computationally efficient method for analyzing ET, particularly in complex scenarios where standard approximations fail.

This study introduces a mixed control design framework for robotic path tracking, integrating sliding mode control (SMC) and trajectory linearizing control (TLC). By employing a nonlinear coordinate transformation, the problem is simplified to regulating a single scalar signal, where SMC and TLC are utilized to handle the control of this signal's derivative and original signal, respectively. The proposed architecture offers superior tracking accuracy compared to conventional SMC designs and is more resilient to disturbances and model uncertainties than standard TLC. Furthermore, the approach is straightforward to implement, requiring only a precise dynamic model of the robot's kinematics.

We introduce a theory describing the vast thermoelectric effect, a phenomenon where a magnetic field significantly boosts electrical resistance in ferromagnetic conductors. This mechanism is driven by the magnetic field's modulation of the spin Seebeck effect, which alters the temperature gradient of the equilibrium magnetization. We demonstrate that the effect's magnitude scales with the square of the applied field, a relationship that holds true for field strengths up to several Tesla. Furthermore, we establish that the effect's intensity is directly proportional to the material's spin Seebeck coefficient and inversely proportional to its magnetic stiffness. Utilizing these principles, we analyzed thin-film samples of the ferromagnetic Heusler alloy Co$_2$MnSi, which exhibit a low stiffness of approximately 0.1 T/Km. Our findings revealed that the effect's size in these films is roughly 100 times greater than in bulk materials with similar composition but much higher stiffness (~10 T/Km). These insights suggest that the vast thermoelectric effect could be harnessed for energy harvesting and actuation in thin-film devices.

This study examines finite fields $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ where $q$ is a prime power and $n$ is a positive integer, focusing on binomial components of degree $d$ where $d$ does not divide $n$. We establish that for any integers $m$ and $k$ satisfying $0 \leq k < n$ and $m > 0$, there exists a specific element $\alpha \in \mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ such that the subfield $\mathbb{F}_{q^k}$ lies within every coset of the binomial component of order $d$ containing $\alpha Q_{m}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the degree of this component is always a multiple of $gcd(d, q^n-1)$.

UPAALL is a renowned model checker for analyzing timed automata, yet it is not widely adopted for the formal verification of source code. This paper introduces a novel methodology for applying UpPaaL to verify program correctness, specifically targeting the validation of temporal properties within resource usage limits. We outline a framework to construct UpPaal models directly from source code, enabling the concurrent execution of multiple program instances to simulate resource constraints. The study demonstrates this approach using a concrete example: a C library handling binary trees.

We introduce a novel, end-to-end deep learning approach that simultaneously optim both the metasurface and the subsequent image reconstruction. The metasurface is designed to generate specific light propagation patterns that complement the recovery algorithm. Theoretically, this joint optimization framework is defined as a non-convex min-max problem, which we address using a min-max gradient descent method. The resulting deep learning model is trained via backpropagation, where the loss function is computed after the final layer of the reconstruction process. Experimental results indicate that this joint optimization strategy yields superior image quality compared to traditional compressed sensing methods that rely on fixed, theoretically derived sparsity constraints.

This study examines the dynamics of a hydrogen atom within a strong bi-color circularly polarized laser field, specifically focusing on AC-Stark-displaced resonances. We demonstrate that these resonances are maintained even under intense laser irradiation, a conclusion drawn from analyzing the energy spectrum of the corresponding dressed states. Furthermore, our findings indicate that these AC-Stark resonances are particularly significant at lower laser frequencies, where AC-Stark effects induce a redshift in the resonant modes.

This paper introduces a novel framework for merging multiple images by integrating both their visual and conceptual elements. We present a new technique that encodes these components as vectors, enabling the construction of image compositions through the linear combination of these semantic elements. We assess the quality of these generated blends by evaluating the visual realism and coherence of the resulting imagery.

Gene expression is inherently stochastic, with fluctuations in protein levels driven by the random occurrence of biochemical reactions. Although the individual steps of these processes are often difficult to observe directly, they can be modeled using chemical kinetic equations. This study presents a computational framework for extracting kinetic parameters from experimental data, specifically single-cell time series, by utilizing a recently developed approximate chemical master equation (ACME). This approach is demonstrated on a synthetic transcription factor circuit, where the inferred rates closely match the ground truth values. Furthermore, the method's utility is validated through its application to real-world data from a synthetic toggle switch.

This paper introduces a data-driven, semi-supervised approach to education, specifically designed to address the challenge of scaling personalized instruction. We begin by defining a data-centric framework for semi-supervised learning within the context of education, which is then applied to a recommendation system aimed at guiding students through educational resources. This system utilizes a combination of content-based information regarding the resources and historical performance data from students. We evaluate the method using a real-world dataset from a massive open online course (MOOC). Our findings indicate that this data-guided semi-supervised learning approach significantly outperforms a standard baseline method.

Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms (QAOA) are quantum variational methods designed to address combinatorial optimization tasks. This study investigates the training dynamics of QAOA when applied to the MaxCut problem, utilizing both classical and quantum simulations. We analyze the impact of training dataset size and training iterations on QAOA's performance, specifically examining how these factors influence the probability of the quantum state collapsing into the optimal solution. Our findings indicate that quantum computing platforms can efficiently and accurately evaluate QAOA's performance, even with noisy data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the maximumCut problem is susceptible to overfitting during training; consequently, larger training datasets are required to achieve high success rates.

Re-identification (ReID) aims to locate specific individuals across multiple camera views within surveillance networks. This task is typically defined as retrieving a set of candidate images containing a particular person when provided with their reference image. However, a more advanced approach involves Individual ReID (IRID), which seeks to pinpoint the exact presence of a specific individual among numerous images. This paper introduces a novel framework for IRID that integrates two key components: a similarity matrix derived from comparing query images with a reference image, and a similarity graph constructed from pairwise image comparisons. By synthesizing insights from both the matrix and graph, the system successfully isolates images belonging to the target individual. Empirical results demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques on standard ReID datasets.

The integration of renewable energy sources into the power grid has led to increased variability and uncertainty, necessitating robust research methodologies to effectively manage these challenges. This study introduces a data-driven approach to time series reconstruction, designed to enhance the quality of data utilized in power systems research. This methodology employs a two-stage process: initially, a generative model is trained on existing time series to learn their underlying patterns; subsequently, the model generates new synthetic data that maintains the original series' characteristics while adhering to specific constraints. This framework proves particularly effective for scenarios involving missing data points or noise, as it can synthesize new samples that are both realistic and compliant with external requirements. This capability is especially valuable for training and validating models in contemporary power systems research, where data quality is critical.

This study introduces a robust-convergence-proof algorithm for the unique solution of a variational inequality problem defined on a closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space, utilizing two families of quasi-nonexpansive mappings. We establish that our proposed method converges robustly to this unique solution under assumptions of the strong monotonicity of the operator, Lipschitz continuity, and quasi-$\kappa$-contractivity of the aforementioned two families of mappings.

This paper investigates the arrangement of geodesics within hyperbolic surfaces equipped with a specific cone metric, where the cone angles are all equal to $\pi(1+1/k)$ for some $k \geq 2$. We demonstrate that the maximal count of geodesic intersections between any pair of simple closed curves adheres to the formula $\frac{1}{2}k(n-2)$, where $n$ represents the count of the surface's boundary components. This result sharpens a previous finding by J. Schaeffer and C. Vernick. We further prove the existence of an isoxial Fuchsian group—defined as a group with uniform hyperbolic elements—that acts on $\mathbb{H}^2$ and possesses fundamental domains isometric to those found on the aforementioned cone surfaces. Finally, we show that the associated reflection group derived from such a group is a polyhedral reflection group with Euclidean geometry.

This study examines the potential lepton flavor violation (LFV) decay mode $\Upsilon (3S)\rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\mp}$, with the aim of establishing a limit on the branching fraction for this LFV process. We calculate the branching fraction for this violation within the framework of the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) by considering the contributions of chargino-squark and neutralino-sneutrino one-loop diagrams. We find that the branching fraction for $\Upsilon (3S)\rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\mp}$ remains negligibly small in the MSSM, rendering it experimentally unobservable with current technology.

The discovery of superconductivity in flat-band Kagome metals has recently gained significant attention. This study examines the pressure-dependent superconducting properties of Pd3P2(S0.5Se0.5)8, a material featuring a Pd-based flat-band Kagome lattice. We report that ambient-pressure superconductivity emerges at Tc = 1.8 K, which increases to 2.6 K under 1.5 GPa of pressure. Notably, the critical temperature (Tc) exhibits a positive pressure coefficient (dTc/dP) across the entire pressure range studied. This positive correlation is attributed to the material's high electronic density of states (DOS) and a substantial N(0)V value, which are consistent with the McMillin equation. Furthermore, we observed a significant enhancement in the electronic specific heat coefficient, gamma, under pressure, suggesting that compressing the lattice increases the electronic DOS. These findings indicate that the lattice compression strengthens the electronic correlations within the flat band, thereby driving superconductivity.

We examine how data regarding a charged, chemically interacting, and evaporating black hole can be retrieved within Jackiw-Teitelboil gravity. This analysis relies on the existence of a specific region within the near-horizon geometry where the curvature is gentle enough to allow for a trustworthy semi-classical treatment. By applying a Euclidean path integral technique to this domain, we derive the one-loop partition function, which acts as a density matrix for the black hole's microstates. Through the implementation of the replica trick, we calculate the von Neumann entropy of this state and demonstrate that it adheres to the first law of black hole thermodynamics.

This paper examines the application of Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs) for regression tasks, where the training data consists of noisy observations of an underlying continuous curve. We introduce a new model that integrates latent variables to address erratic and missing data points within such noisy observations. We demonstrate that the gradients of this model remain well-behaved and support back-propagation, even when the data contains irregularities and gaps. We also establish that the model's loss function is lower-bounded by a function that decreases exponentially fast as the number of noisy observations is reduced. We support these theoretical findings with experiments on synthetic datasets, confirming that the model effectively recovers underlying continuous curves despite containing up to 90\% noisy data points.

This study introduces the Object Recall Transformer (ORTR), a transformer-based architecture designed for object-oriented target navigation. ORTR integrates visual and language features to predict the next robot action. It employs a transformer encoder to generate language-conditioned visual representations, which are subsequently processed by a transformer decoder to forecast the upcoming state. Unlike prior research that relies on 3D scene understanding, ORTR operates entirely on 2D image sequences, thereby eliminating the need for explicit 3D scene reconstruction. This approach enhances scalability and transferability across different environments. Empirical evaluations across two benchmarks demonstrate that ORTR surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 10.1% and 13.1% increase in success rates for the IndoorNav and Navigation benchmarks, respectively.

Large pre-trained language models are typically fine-tuned on numerous tasks, yet this approach is often impractical due to the high costs associated with the time and data required. Consequently, Meta-Optimization for Instruction-based Task Learning (OPT-IML) has emerged as a viable alternative. This method leverages a single, extensive pre-trained model to learn how to adapt to new instructions, enabling it to generate instructions that align with the intended task. We introduce OPT-IML, a framework that utilizes a pre-trained model to learn instruction generation from a small set of examples, thereby eliminating the need for task-specific fine-tuning. Our approach incorporates a Generalization Loss function, which ensures that the model can produce instructions that generalize effectively to unseen examples within the same task. We evaluate OPT-IML against state-of-the-art Meta-learning methods using a comprehensive suite of benchmarks, including natural language understanding, question answering, and text classification. The results demonstrate that OPT-IML achieves performance comparable to current best-in-class Meta-learning approaches.

Scratch, a prominent visual programming platform for children, empowers users to construct, share, and collaborate on interactive stories, games, and art. While the site's official guidelines mandate that creators be at least seven years old, the platform's accessibility draws users of all ages, including those who fall below this threshold. Researchers have identified Scratch as a valuable environment for developing computational thinking and programming skills, yet the platform's inability to verify ages creates a challenge in assessing whether creators have grasped these concepts. Consequently, the study investigates how a creator's periphery—defined by their age, gender, and geographic location—impacts the complexity of their projects. Analyzing 10,000 submissions from children aged five to nine, the findings reveal that creators from the United States tend to produce more intricate projects than their peers elsewhere. Additionally, the data indicates that while gender does not significantly influence project difficulty, age does; specifically, five-year-olds consistently generate simpler outputs compared to eight and nine-year-olds.

This study introduces a novel approach to calculating disturbances in the uniform electron fluid, utilizing transcorrelated Hamiltonians and the R-NSPT method. By leveraging the R-NSPT framework, we successfully incorporate the effects of the phonon-shifted (PC) Hamiltonian. Consequently, we derive analytical formulas for the energy disturbances up to the fourth order, which explicitly incorporate the electron correlation function. Numerical evaluations of these results for systems with varying electron numbers demonstrate that the PC Hamiltonian significantly enhances convergence speed.

We introduce a method for generating covariance matrices for object tracking, utilizing only positional uncertainty data and enabling the tracking of physical objects. This approach employs optimal transport to derive covariance matrices from positional samples, incorporating observed physical constraints to ensure physical validity. Additionally, we demonstrate that covariance matrices can be estimated directly from optimal transport metrics. We validate the method's effectiveness through experiments on indoor and outdoor datasets, comparing our results against established tracking algorithms.

The rapid expansion of Big Data has driven the creation of numerous data mining algorithms, yet the inherent privacy risks within these datasets have sparked significant concern. This paper introduces a new privacy-preserving framework for Big Data tensor analysis, designed to protect sensitive information while enabling collaborative computation across multiple parties. The proposed method employs randomized tensor network decomposition to generate randomized tensor factorization, which is subsequently processed through a distributed Tucker decomposition to produce a final, approximate result. The authors demonstrate that this randomized Tucker decomposition preserves the original data's essential characteristics, ensuring that the resulting low-rank approximation remains highly accurate. Furthermore, the framework incorporates differential privacy to safeguard against privacy breaches. Experimental results confirm that the method effectively balances privacy protection with data utility, achieving high accuracy in the recovered low-rank approximation.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven highly effective for training robots to execute complex tasks. However, the significant gap between simulated environments and the real world often leads to poor performance when simulators fail to capture real-world dynamics. To address this, we introduce SafeAPT, a novel framework designed to ensure safe and robust policy transfer from simulation to reality. SafeAPT generates a diverse set of policies by training multiple agents in parallel within separate simulated environments. This approach allows the system to adapt to real-world conditions upon deployment, thereby enhancing the likelihood of success. We evaluated SafeAPT on a real-world robotic arm tasked with placing a cylinder into a cup. Experimental results demonstrate that SafeAPT achieves a 90% success rate, outperforming the standard transfer method, which succeeded in only 10% of trials.

This study presents an observational analysis of jets within radio galaxies and quasars, utilizing data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). The primary objective is to investigate the physical characteristics of these jets, specifically examining their collimation and the presence of kinks. We define collimation as the ratio of the maximum jet radius to the distance along the jet, while a kink is identified as a localized region where the jet axis changes direction. Our findings indicate that jets in radio galaxies and quasars are generally narrow, with the vast majority of their radii remaining under 100 kpc. Furthermore, jets in radio galaxies are more likely to exhibit kinks compared to those in quasars. We also observe that the collimation of jets in radio galaxies varies with redshift, whereas no such trend is detected for quasars. These results align with the hypothesis that radio jets in galaxies are primarily confined by the surrounding interstellar medium, while in quasar jets, the dominant factor is likely the Lorentz force.

This study introduces a novel time-varying nonlinear time series regression model designed to analyze time series data exhibiting both temporal dynamics and nonlinear characteristics. The proposed methodology employs a sieve approach to approximate the unknown, time-varying nonlinear function using a series expansion, while simultaneously accounting for temporal shifts via a time-varying autoregressive component. By integrating a partial least squares algorithm with a sieve framework, we develop a new inference method that effectively handles high-dimensional covariates and evolving nonlinearities. Theoretical analysis confirms the method's consistency and establishes a minimax optimal convergence rate for the nonlinear function estimation. Additionally, a simulation study validates the method's superior performance in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency compared to existing alternatives, with a subsequent application demonstrating the method's practical utility in analyzing the volatility of US stock returns.

This paper investigates the identification of aggressive language within social media content. We introduce a new, comprehensive dataset for this task, which includes 1,000 manually annotated tweets. We also develop a robust neural network architecture designed to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the proposed dataset. Additionally, we evaluate our model against the Aggressive Language Identification dataset from the 2018 ACL Workshop on Multitask Learning, demonstrating that it outperforms all existing models from that competition.

Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) is a non-invasive technique for mapping brain activity, with functional connectivity (FC) analysis serving as a primary method for investigating the brain's functional architecture. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to extract the latent structure of FC patterns from fMRI data. Our approach utilizes a graph convolutional network (GCN) to learn a low-dimensional representation of FC, which is then used to identify the intrinsic dimensionality of the FC manifold. By applying this method to a dataset of 1,000 fMRI scans from the Human Connectome Project, we discovered that FC can be effectively represented within a 10-dimensional space. Furthermore, we observed that the dimensionality of the FC manifold varies across different subjects.

This study introduces a unified framework based on dissipativity to analyze the convergence of Nesterov's accelerated methods for minimizing smooth, strongly convex functions. By utilizing a specific Lyapunov function, we demonstrate that the method maintains a descent property, ensuring convergence to the unique optimal solution. Furthermore, we establish that the method attains an improved rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$, which represents an enhancement over the standard rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$.

This study introduces a new numerical framework designed to address boundary conditions in hyperbolic systems featuring source terms, utilizing an implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta (IMEXRK) method. The approach treats the source term component explicitly and the wave propagation component implicitly. We propose a boundary treatment strategy wherein the implicit step accounts for wave propagation from interior points to the boundary, while boundary waves are generated in the explicit step. This method is applied to the shallow water equations, and its accuracy is validated through two test cases: the Riemann problem and a dam-break scenario.

Silicon photovoltaics are widely regarded as the leading technology for solar energy, yet their potential for capturing sunlight is constrained by the thickness of the material. While light-trapping strategies have proven effective in boosting absorption within thin-film devices, this study introduces a novel 3D photonic crystal (PhC) architecture designed to enhance light capture in ultrathin silicon membranes. This approach utilizes a distributed Bragg reflector (DBR) as the substrate and incorporates a 3D PhC layer on the membrane's opposing surface. The PhC structure is optimized to couple incoming light into high-quality-factor (Q) modes, thereby extending the optical path length and increasing absorption. Numerical simulations confirm that this 3D PhC design outperforms traditional 1D reflectors, achieving an absorption rate of 90% in a 20 nm silicon layer at 600 nm. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that absorption can be further enhanced by integrating the PhC with a DBR, a method that yields an absorption rate of 95% in a 20 nm silicon layer at 600 nm.

In MRUA, a model must evaluate the credibility of various potential outcomes based on input data, where the true outcome remains ambiguous. Current top-K recommendation systems typically rely on nearest-neighbor strategies, which calculate distances between user and item embeddings using a specific metric. However, these methods often fail to capture the full complexity of user preferences, particularly when users exhibit diverse tastes. To address this, we introduce a new approach that employs a probabilistic model to measure user-user similarity. This method leverages a learned margin to distinguish between similar and dissimilar users, thereby refining the similarity assessment. Furthermore, we develop an efficient sampling algorithm to support the probabilistic framework, which enables the simultaneous optimization of both the model parameters and the margin. Extensive experiments on standard datasets demonstrate that our technique significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

Quantum channels are typically characterized by a set of parameters that define their input-output behavior. In the non-Markovian context, these parameters vary with time, a phenomenon that can be quantified through a measure capturing the monotonicity of a specific quantum property. This work investigates a broad class of non-unital channels, termed conduits, and demonstrates that non-Markovianity inherent to them persists across all time scales. We introduce a non-Markovian measure that remains constant for any fixed quantum conduit, providing definitive proof of time-remnant non-Markovity. We also present a quantifiable metric for the magnitude of this effect, which allows for the derivation of lower and upper bounds on its value.

This study introduces a method for categorizing unlabeled data into established groups by employing a counterfactual framework. The proposed approach first trains a model to interpret the reasons behind sample assignments, followed by utilizing active learning to iteratively refine these explanations using newly labeled samples. The effectiveness of this strategy is demonstrated through experiments on two real-world datasets.

Semantic mapping is a critical area within robotics, yet the absence of a standardized benchmark hinders the objective comparison of various algorithms. To address this, we introduce RoSmEEry, a novel framework designed for the rigorous assessment and evaluation of semantic mapping techniques. This framework relies on a library of pre-defined simulated robotic scenarios, enabling the creation of diverse test environments to evaluate algorithms under varying conditions. We present a comprehensive suite of these scenarios, ranging from basic environments to complex ones featuring specific challenges like dynamic objects, occlusions, and limited sensor data. Furthermore, we conduct an extensive comparative analysis of state-of-the-art semantic mapping algorithms across these scenarios. This study aims to offer a foundational benchmark for the field, facilitating the identification of promising solutions and uncovering avenues for future research.

Rikudo is a newly introduced puzzle in which the objective is to complete a grid by filling in missing cells so that every row and column contains exactly one of each of the four colors. While determining the feasibility of a completed grid for a given puzzle instance is NP-complete, we demonstrate that Rikudo specifically falls within this complexity class, proving its general solvability problem to be NP-hard.

Optimal transport (OT) is a mathematical framework for quantifying the disparity between two probability distributions. It has recently gained significant traction in machine learning, particularly in applications like generative modeling and domain adaptation. However, the standard OT formulation is NP-hard, making it computationally prohibitive for large-scale applications. This overview examines the primary methods for solving OT problems, with a specific focus on efficient numerical techniques for large-scale problems. We begin by establishing the mathematical foundations of OT and the discrete linear programming framework. Subsequently, we explore the dual of this linear program, which offers a more efficient approach. Furthermore, we analyze the entropic regularization of the dual problem, a strategy that enables the rapid computation of the Sinkhorn distance. Finally, we discuss the Wasserstein barycenter, a concept that calculates the "average" of multiple distributions, and present the Lloyd algorithm for its computation.

Ramanujan's work on modular equations and identities is explored through the lens of Hecke group theory, specifically utilizing Hecke's $q$-difference operators to derive identities concerning the modular lambda function. This paper presents a novel method for transforming the Hecke collection of $q$-difference equations into algebraic $q'$s, which are subsequently linked to the modular ratios $k$ and $k'$. Furthermore, we introduce a new approach to proving Ramanujan's identities by leveraging the fact that these modular identities are essentially polynomial expressions in $k$ and $k'$.

We present the first redshift and velocity dispersion measurements for 24 galaxies within 8 lensing systems, utilizing Keck Observatory data. By analyzing the redshifts of these lenses, we derive the first independent estimates of the lensing mass and velocity dispersions for the host galaxies. These findings are compared with previous results from the TDCOSMO collaboration, which utilized the lensing galaxies themselves to constrain the Hubble constant ($H_0$). We find that our new measurements align well with prior data, with the exception of one system where a significant discrepancy exists. This outlier is likely due to a misidentified stellar population in the earlier analysis. We also observe a systematic offset in the redshifts of the lenses in system Q0957+560, which we attribute to the presence of a faint, undetected satellite galaxy. We further investigate the relationship between the redshifts of the lensing galaxies and the mass of the dark matter halos, finding a correlation that is consistent with theoretical predictions. This study introduces a novel technique for solving nonlinear time scale $q$-fractional differential equations, which are also referred to as $q$-dynamic equations. The proposed approach relies on the $q$-chain rule and $q$-fractional integration by parts. A key advantage of this method is that it requires no initial approximation, making it a straightforward and effective tool for addressing this class of equations. Furthermore, the technique is broadly applicable to various types of equations, including those with nonconstant arguments, standard initial value problems, and the $q$-fractional wave equation.

The Hall effect is a cornerstone of condensed matter physics, with its behavior in various systems often traced back to topological invariants. This study investigates the topological nature of the Hall conductivity induced by phonons. We demonstrate that the phonon Hall effect's Hall conductivity is quantized in the limit of a large system size, and that this parameter transforms as a Chern number under adiabatic deformations that preserve the effect's existence. These findings are corroborated by numerical simulations.

We introduce a novel approach for acquiring hyperspectral images, which we term Broad Field Spectral Imaging using Shifted Excitation Raman Difference Spectroscopy (BFSERSIDS). This technique integrates the capabilities of both Shaded Excitation Raman Imaging (SERDS) and the nod-and-shuffle method. In this setup, a single spectrally resolved camera captures images from a Nod-and-Shuffle spectrometer, which is illuminated by a laser source that is alternately shifted between two frequencies. By shifting the laser wavelength in opposite directions across two adjacent spectral channels, the resulting spectral response of the target is inherently corrected for both instrumental and spatial variations. This strategy effectively mitigates the need for complex calibration procedures. The proposed method was experimentally validated using a commercial push-broom hyperspectral camera to analyze a printed circuit board (PCB) sample. The findings demonstrate that BFSERSIDS offers significant advantages, including the ability to acquire hyperspectral data rapidly, the elimination of the need for reference standards, and the ability to correct for system imperfections without additional calibration.

This study establishes Fejér and Levin-Stec kin inequalities for finite matrices, with specific focus on their applications to the Cauchy product of series as well as convolution operations involving sequences and functions.

We investigate the mean null energy condition (MNEC) within holographic evaporating black holes, which are defined by a black brane geometry featuring a time-dependent, horizon-dependent redshift factor. Our findings indicate that while the null energy violation at the horizon necessitates a compensatory violation of the MNE in the deep interior, this alignment precisely matches recent findings derived from semiclassical calculations.

This work outlines the essential components of a unitary, two-dimensional (2d) conformal field theory (CFT), specifically focusing on the OPE structure and the framework of crossing symmetry. We demonstrate that these concepts are instrumental in deriving the 4-point function, utilizing a 2d 16-vertex model as an illustrative example.

Industrial Control Systems (ICS) are increasingly integrated into critical infrastructure, making them attractive targets for cyberattacks. To address this, researchers have introduced various detection and prevention mechanisms, yet the lack of a unified standard for cybersecurity evaluation has hindered the widespread adoption of these solutions. This paper introduces the Cybersecurity Threat Modeling for Industrial Control Systems (ICS-CTM2) framework, which enables the assessment of cybersecurity threats against ICS. Utilizing this framework, we developed an evaluation model for ICS cybersecurity that incorporates diverse ICS components and their associated security threats. This model facilitates the identification of vulnerable ICS elements and threat actors, allowing for the calculation of an overall cybersecurity risk score. Furthermore, we outline a systematic methodology for evaluating the ICS cybersecurity risk score.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is a rapidly expanding field that has seen significant progress in recent years. However, the majority of current MARL algorithms are limited to specific tasks, such as zero-sum or constant-sum games, and often fail to perform well in more complex scenarios. To address this, we introduce a new MARL framework centered on "Avaricious-based Value Representation" (AVR). This approach enables agents to learn a shared value function, where individual agents derive their own assessments of the global value by considering the impact of their own actions on others. We demonstrate that this method is versatile and can be applied to diverse tasks, including those with variable-sum and complex dynamics. Experimental results indicate that AVRs outperform existing state-of-the-art algorithms in handling these broader scenarios.

Pretrained language models (PLMs) are frequently assessed using metrics like adversarial robustness, data reconstruction, and downstream performance. However, this study introduces StereoSet, a new benchmark designed to measure PLMs' susceptibility to gender and stereotypical associations. The evaluation reveals that even large-scale models struggle to effectively eliminate these biases. Furthermore, the work demonstrates that standard fine-tuning strategies offer only negligible improvements in reducing such biases.

Optimizing the tilt of electric insulators is critical for maintaining high-quality electrical performance and extending the lifespan of insulators in high-voltage transmission lines. However, the complexity of the task, combined with the high costs and risks associated with manual adjustments, has necessitated the development of automated systems. While existing literature has extensively covered the positioning of insulators within these systems, the specific challenge of optimizing tilt remains largely unaddressed. This paper introduces a practical approach to tilt optimization that relies on data collected from robots performing routine inspections. By utilizing data-driven methods, this study leverages the existing data to train a policy for optimal tilt configuration, even when the data originates from policies that do not follow the target distribution. This capability is achieved through off-policy learning techniques, which allow for the efficient use of available information. Furthermore, the study employs a deep reinforcement learning framework to develop a policy that outperforms the current industry standard.

The CKM angle $\gamma$ is determined through a combination of two LHCb measurements involving $B$ meson decays. These analyses include a time-dependent study of $B^0 \to K^+ K^- \pi^+ \pi^-$ and a $SU(3)$ flavor symmetry-based combination of $B^0$ and $B^+$ decays into $K^+ K^-$ and $\pi^+ \pi^-$ final states. The resulting value for $\gamma$ is $73.9^\circ \pm 5.8^\circ$.

This study examines the complex symmetries of ellipsoids defined over specific finite fields, particularly those of the form $\mathcal{E}(\mathbb{F}_q) = \{x \in \mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_q) : x^T A x = 1\}$, where $A$ is a symmetric matrix. We demonstrate that the group of automorphisms for $\mathcal{E}$ is isomorphic to the orthogonal group $O(3,q)$ relative to the matrix $A$. Furthermore, the paper explores connections between these complex symmetries and the combinatorial properties of ellipsoids.

Contemporary data markets are characterized by a fundamental imbalance: private entities collect personal data from individuals who are often unaware of the data's scope, the entities that receive it, or the intended uses. This disparity in information is widely considered a primary driver of ethical breaches, including privacy violations and data misuse. This paper investigates how individuals perceive this informational imbalance and whether such views influence their behavior. We conducted a survey of 1,000 participants representing the general public, social media users, and professionals within the data industry. Our findings reveal that while respondents are generally skeptical of how corporations utilize personal data, they also recognize the necessity of data access for corporate innovation. Consequently, participants favor a model of data sharing that involves transparency and compensation. We conclude by discussing the implications of these insights for designing data markets that are both ethical and effective.

This study introduces a Deep Learning-driven List Sphere Decoding (DL-LSD) algorithm tailored for Faster-than-Nyquist (FTN) signaling. By utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from the received signal, the proposed method constructs a feature vector that is then processed by an LSD module to determine the optimal set of candidate symbol sequences. This approach effectively mitigates the FTN signal interference. Simulation results demonstrate that DL-LSD achieves superior performance compared to conventional methods, specifically offering a gain of 0.5 dB at a bit error rate (BER) of 10⁻³ for FTN signaling with a 0.5 overlap factor, and an additional gain of 0.2 dB for an overlap factor of 0.75.

This work presents the order topology on impact algebras and establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for this topology to be compatible with the impact algebra structure, thereby defining what constitutes an impact compactly generated space. It is demonstrated that compactly generated points in this category are precisely those impact algebras featuring an underlying compact Hausdorff order topology. The study defines an impact Frink topology as the order topology derived from an impact algebra where every impact interval possesses a supremum. It is proven that an impact Frink topology is compatible if and only if the impact algebra is Frink complete, leading to the conclusion that compact Hausdorff impact Frink topologies correspond exactly to complete impact algebras.

Data augmentation is a fundamental technique for enhancing the generalization of machine learning models, particularly in computer vision. While traditional methods like random cropping and flipping are effective, they often fail to generate diverse training samples. To address this, we introduce SaliencyMix, a novel augmentation strategy that leverages saliency maps to guide the mixing of images. This approach identifies salient regions across pairs of images and blends the corresponding areas, ensuring that the resulting augmented samples are both diverse and semantically significant. We evaluated SaliencyMix on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, comparing it against conventional and saliency-guided baselines. Results indicate that SaliencyMix consistently boosts generalization performance, with the most significant improvements observed in scenarios involving limited training data.

We examine properties of certain (potentially infinite) Iwahori-Hecke algebras $\mathcal{H}(G)$, where $G$ is a finitely generated group. We demonstrate that if $\mathcal{H}(G)$ admits an infinite set of irreducible representations, then it cannot support any non-tracial elements. Furthermore, we identify specific instances where $\mathcal{H}(G)$ is known to possess a unique Hecke trace.

Intrinsic alignments (IA) of galaxies within galaxy clusters are a significant source of systematic error in weak lensing studies. This paper investigates how varying the strength of gravitational interactions influences IA strength, specifically by testing a modified (Hörendesi) gravity model against the standard $\Lambda$CDM baseline. Our analysis reveals that the observed IA signal is highly sensitive to the speed of gravitational waves, which itself changes in modified gravity frameworks. By combining measurements of the IA signal with those of cosmic shear and cosmic distortion, we constrain the parameter $\alpha$—which quantifies the deviation from general relativity—to a range of $-0.1 < \alpha < 0.1$ at a 95\% confidence level.

The paper investigates the rheological behavior of soft, deformable particles in both two and three dimensions, specifically focusing on systems where the ratio of the particle's bending stiffness to its surface tension is low. These conditions result in a spontaneous formation of folds within the particles. The authors demonstrate that the rheological properties of such systems are governed by the magnitude of the applied shear rate, as well as the specific values of the bending stiffness and surface tension. Furthermore, it is shown that the steady-state rheological response is non-monotonic with respect to shear rate, exhibiting a maximum at a specific critical shear rate. The study also analyzes the transition from a steady state to a limit cycle, noting that the critical shear rate for this instability is non-monotonic relative to variations in the bending stiffness and surface tension. The authors conclude that these findings have significant implications for the rheological characteristics of biological cells and other deformable objects.

This study introduces a data-driven approach to model the melting of gold nanoparticles, leveraging a coarse-grained potential derived from extensive molecular dynamics simulations. By utilizing a single potential to describe both solid and liquid phases, the model captures the first-order melting transition, including coexistence between phases and the influence of finite-size effects. The melting temperature is determined by the interplay between surface and bulk contributions, which are modeled as functions of the particle's radius. This interaction is expressed through a logistic function fitted to simulation data, allowing for the prediction of melting temperatures for larger particles that exceed current computational simulation limits. The proposed framework is broadly applicable to various spherical nanoparticles, extending beyond gold.

This paper establishes the existence of multiple solutions for regular bifurcation theory involving potential operators, where the operators depend on a parameter in a singular manner. Our findings extend classical results by Rabinowitz and Krasnosel'skii to accommodate singular dependencies. Additionally, we present existence theorems for boundary value problems related to the Laplace operator defined on exterior domains.

The Standard Model of particle physics identifies the three fermion generations as a fundamental mystery. This study proposes that the existence of these three generations arises from a deeper structure, specifically a "tetrahedron of flavors." This geometric construct is defined by an SU(3) symmetry acting upon three elementary "tastes": Red, Blue, and Green. This framework offers a novel explanation for the origin of fermion masses and the specific values of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix. Notably, it predicts a relationship between the CKM angle $\gamma$ and the electron mass, expressed as $\gamma = \arccos(m_e/m_e)$, which aligns with experimental data. Furthermore, the model accounts for the non-zero neutrino mixing angle $\theta_{13}$ and suggests the presence of a new particle, $\Delta$, possessing a mass of $10^{16}$ GeV.

This study establishes several notable identities pertaining to (h,q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials with a weight parameter α, utilizing the umbral calculus approach combined with the non-commutive Wick algebra within the umbral framework.

Estimating the long-term impact of psychotherapy is a significant challenge in mental health research. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning framework designed to estimate long-term therapy effects by modeling the therapy process as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). We propose a novel approach that utilizes the optimal state-value function to forecast long-term outcomes. This method is validated using a dataset from a randomized controlled trial (RCT) involving cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for depression. The results demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms existing methods, which are limited to using only the final post-treatment assessment.

In retrospective case-control studies, remembrance bias (or rememory distortion) occurs when participants inaccurately recall or misrepresent their past exposures or risk factors. This study introduces a novel methodology for utilizing such data in causal inference. The approach integrates both case and control group data with self-reports from participants regarding the likelihood of memory distortion, categorized as high or low. By applying the G-computation formula, the method estimates the effect of a treatment on an outcome among those whose remembrance distortion is either high or low. Furthermore, it estimates the average treatment effect within both subgroups. The proposed framework is validated through a simulation study and a practical application involving a case-control investigation into the link between smoking and lung cancer.

Generative models have become a cornerstone of modern machine learning, offering a wide array of applications ranging from image and audio synthesis to natural language processing. However, training these models remains a computationally demanding task. This paper introduces a novel architecture for generative autoencoders that integrates invertible layers, enabling the use of maximum likelihood training with exact likelihood calculations. We demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art models by significant margins in both training efficiency and generative quality.

The Internet of Things (IoT) has enabled the collection of vast amounts of urban data, facilitating the analysis of feature patterns within these datasets. However, the sheer volume of this data makes it difficult for humans to comprehend and derive insights. This paper introduces a visualization method designed to aid in the examination of urban data. It employs a matrix-based approach to depict feature patterns, utilizing an intelligent algorithm to automatically identify and visualize significant features. The method is evaluated through experiments on datasets from smart cities, traffic networks, and energy grids, with findings indicating that it effectively supports the analysis of feature patterns in urban data.

This study introduces a novel geometric multigrid preconditioner tailored for discretized Darcy flow, generalized Stokes systems, and reaction-diffusion equations using discontinuous Galerkin finite element methods (DG-P0). The approach employs a two-scale strategy: an implicit fine-scale component and an explicit coarse-scale component. The resulting preconditioner is both robust and efficient, maintaining a constant condition number relative to problem parameters and achieving rapid convergence with a fixed number of iterations. Theoretical analysis is complemented by numerical experiments that confirm the preconditioner's efficacy.

Missing data remains a significant challenge in statistical analysis, as the absence of information can compromise the validity of conclusions. This study introduces a Bayesian approach to handling missing values by evaluating a range of potential missing data mechanisms. The primary objective is to determine whether findings remain consistent across various plausible assumptions regarding missing data patterns. This work presents a novel method for missing data sensitivity analysis within the Bayesian framework, utilizing a prior distribution for a parameter that governs the missing data mechanism. This strategy enables the assessment of multiple missing data scenarios simultaneously. Furthermore, we develop a metric to evaluate sensitivity to these assumptions, specifically the e-value, which represents the ratio of posterior to prior probability for a given parameter. This metric facilitates a comprehensive evaluation of sensitivity to missing data assumptions. Finally, we demonstrate the proposed methodology using a simulation study and apply it to real-world data.

In multivariate crossover trials, researchers often utilize repeated measures to evaluate treatment effects. However, when data are missing due to dropout, the resulting incomplete data structure can introduce bias if not properly handled. To address this, we propose a novel approach for assessing missing information in multivariate settings. This method involves calculating, for each subject, the likelihood that their observed data would occur under both the null and alternative hypotheses. We then apply a permutation test to compare the resulting likelihood ratios. Through a simulation study, we demonstrate that this proposed test maintains the correct Type I error rate under the null hypothesis. Furthermore, we illustrate the method using an example from a multivariate crossover trial involving the treatment of schizophrenia.

This paper presents a novel polyhedral framework linked to weak 2-categories, which generalizes the concept of the lattice polytope found in the work of Fei and Fei. The vertices of this framework correspond to specific types of feeble functors, while its 1-skeleton is shown to be the 1-category of these structures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the combinatorial structure of this framework is governed by a unique algebraic property, which is a generalization of the property that the lattice polyto

The integration of novel features and optimizations within the memory hierarchy necessitates a platform capable of accommodating diverse in-memory applications. To address this, we introduce CODIC, an affordable and flexible in-memory substrate designed to enable customized functionality. By utilizing a NoC-based approach, the substrate facilitates the development of modular in-memory applications, thereby reducing the time and effort required to design, implement, and assess such solutions. CODIC is compatible with standard FPGA-based NoC infrastructure, leveraging the FPGA's inherent flexibility to support various experimental in-memory scenarios. We demonstrate the substrate's utility through three case studies: a) a machine learning inference engine, b) a distributed hash table, and c) a distributed key-value store.

This article serves as the concluding segment of a two-part series examining the administration and orchestration of virtualized network assets. In the first installment, we introduced the foundational principles of network virtualization alongside an overview of functional programming. This second part applies that programming paradigm specifically to the challenges inherent in network evolution and design. We begin by addressing the evolution of network technologies, exploring the transition from physical to virtual environments, the criticality of network automation, and the specific hurdles posed by virtualized assets. Subsequently, we outline design principles for these virtualized assets, emphasizing the need for a cohesive, structured approach to network virtualization. This methodology must be guided by functional programming to ensure effective orchestration and management.

The toric code serves as a foundational model for topological quantum computation, a field that has garnered significant attention due to its potential for fault-tolerant operations. While the standard model relies on the Z₂ gauge group, extending it to non-Abelian cases like SU(2) offers a more versatile framework. This study examines the SU(2) gauge-invariant toric code, focusing on the construction of logical qubits and the implementation of fundamental quantum gates. We demonstrate that, despite the increased complexity of the non-Abelian setting, the resulting logical qubits and associated gate operations remain equivalent to those in the standard Abelian toric code. Furthermore, we introduce a protocol for generating Greenberger-Horne-Zemany-Kosten-Slater (GHZ) states using the non-Abelian model, highlighting a distinct advantage of this approach.

The VO Infrastructure Development Team has engineered OPUS, an open-source workflow management system designed for Virtual Organizations. This tool is built upon established VO standards, including the Common VO Application Interface (cVAPI) and the Data Management (DM) API. OPUS offers a suite of features essential for virtual organizations, such as job submission, execution monitoring, and data access. This paper outlines OPUS's design and implementation, with a particular focus on the common components that enable its deployment across diverse Virtual Organizations. Furthermore, we examine various applications developed using the OPES toolkit, which facilitates the creation of customized jobs within the OPUS environment.

This paper introduces a novel digital game designed to boost student engagement and learning outcomes in complex technical subjects. The game, "Network Defense," immerses users in a role as a network defender tasked with identifying and neutralizing intrusions within a wireless system. To achieve this, learners must apply key concepts in wireless networking and signal processing, including signal modulation, signal-to-noise ratio, and signal processing techniques. The study presents the game's design methodology, along with empirical findings from a controlled experiment comparing its effectiveness against traditional instruction methods. The results indicate that participants who engaged with the digital game demonstrated significantly superior performance in both the acquisition and retention of the core technical concepts.

Ozone (O3) serves as a critical tool for detecting and constraining molecular oxygen (O2) in Earth's atmosphere and potentially in exoplanetary atmospheres. This study examines the O2-O3 relationship within Earth-like terrestrial environments, specifically focusing on scenarios where the O2 abundance is low. We demonstrate that the O2-O3 relationship is governed by the balance between photochemical destruction and biological replenishment of O2. Consequently, the O3/O2 ratio is not fixed but can vary significantly, ranging from 10^-4 to 10^-1. This variability arises because biological sources of O2 are not limited to photolysis-driven production; they also include the chemical oxidation of carbon monoxide (CO), a process that sustains O2 levels independently of ozone concentrations. Furthermore, we find that biological O2 production rates are highly sensitive to the photodissociation rate of water vapor (H2O). This dependency is a key factor in shaping atmospheric chemistry and underscores the necessity of accounting for H2O photolysis when modeling O2-O3 dynamics. Ultimately, these findings indicate that O3 is a poor proxy for determining O2 abundances in Earth-like worlds, particularly those with low H2O photolysis rates.

We investigate surface states within the 3D twisted bilayer graphene (TBLG) model, which is characterized by a pseudo-magnetic field derived from an applied perpendicular electric field. This system exhibits a Hofstadter-like spectrum featuring a ground state with crystalline order and a substantial energy gap. We identify a surface current flowing along the crystal facets, which is robust against disorder and persists even in the presence of the large bulk energy gap. This phenomenon is attributed to the unique topology of the surface band structure, which possesses a non-trivial Chern number. We anticipate that our findings will significantly advance the study of surface states in twisted bilayer graphene.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has proven highly effective for general multilingual translation, yet its application to domain-specific fields like medicine remains underexplored. This study evaluates the impact of retraining general MNL-NMT models on medical corpora across various languages. We demonstrate that domain-specific pretraining significantly enhances translation quality for medical text compared to using generic multilingual models.

This study investigates the propagation of ion-acoustic waves in a plasma featuring both nonthermal electrons and positively charged heavy ions. The analysis incorporates the effects of finite ion fluid temperature and the influence of positive ions on the formation of solitary waves and shocks. By employing the reductive perturbation technique, the authors derive the Korteweg-de Vries-Zakharov-Kuznetsov (KZV) equation to determine the phase speed, amplitude, and spatial extent of these waves. The results indicate that positively charged ions can support both compressive and expansive solitary waves, with the inclusion of ion-acoustic temperature favoring the generation of expansive solitary waves. Furthermore, the presence of nonthermal electrons is found to be essential for the existence of expansive solitary waves. The findings also demonstrate that the properties of ion-acoustic waves depend on the density and temperature profiles of the various plasma constituents.

This study introduces a novel approach to pretrain sentence embedding models for multi-lingual dense retrieval, designed to enhance the semantic representation of sentences by incorporating contextual information from surrounding paragraphs. We propose a new unsupervised pretraining framework that utilizes the semantic gap between sentences within the same paragraph as supervision, thereby establishing more robust embedding models. Additionally, we introduce a new pretraining objective called Context-Aware Contrastive Language Image Pre-training (CoCa), which aligns with the dense retrieval task by directly optimizing the semantic distance between embeddings of sentences from the same paragraph. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models on multiple benchmarks, including MS MARCO, TREC, and STS-B, for English, and substantially improves performance on MMR, TREC, and STS-B for English, as well as on MMR, TREC, and STS-B for English, as well as on MMR, TREC, and STS-B for English, as well as on MMR, TREC, and STS-B for English, as well as on MMR, TREC, and STS-B for English, as well as on MMR, TREC, and STS-B for English, as well as on MMR, TREC, and STS-B for English, as well as on MMR, TREC, and STS-B for English, as well as on MMR, TREC, and STS-B

Multimodal educational datasets are essential for advancing research in intelligent tutoring systems, yet they are frequently characterized by significant class imbalance. This imbalance hinders the development of models that can generalize effectively to unseen class distributions. To address this, we introduce Prototypical Mode Rebalance (PMR), a novel data augmentation technique that leverages both semantic and modal information. Specifically, PMR constructs a virtual mode domain by drawing samples from the real-world mode and identifying their nearest neighbors within that synthetic space. These neighbors are then projected back to the real mode, where they are utilized to generate new data instances. We evaluated PMR across three distinct tasks: text-to-image generation, image captioning, and text-to-image caption generation. Experimental results demonstrate that PMR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 1.5% improvement in accuracy for text-to-image generation and a 1.5% improvement in accuracy for image captioning.

Vector engagement theory offers a framework for analyzing the stability of formations within self-organized systems, such as robotic swarms, by employing a vector-based approach. This method is particularly advantageous for systems where individual agents communicate with a limited number of neighbors, as it simplifies the analysis of stability in these networked structures. The approach is applied to a specific class of swarm control algorithms, including the widely used Cyclic Vector (CV) algorithm. In CV, agents transmit their desired velocity to a neighboring subset, and each agent adjusts its own velocity based on this information. This paper extends vector engagement theory to account for scenarios involving variable neighbor counts and demonstrates its utility in analyzing the stability of CV algorithms. The study establishes sufficient conditions for CV stability, which are notably less restrictive than existing results. These findings are further illustrated through numerical simulations.

This study introduces a Tensor-Train Network (TTN)-based approach for spoken command recognition, utilizing a dataset from the command25 subset of the Google Speech Commands 1.0 dataset. The architecture employs a Tensor-Train (TT) layer to extract features from the input data, which are then processed by a standard Neural Network (NN) to generate the final output. The model's performance was evaluated using three distinct training strategies: 1) training the entire network end-to-end, 2) pre-training the Tensor-Train layer before fine-tuning the NN, and 3) pre-training the Tensor-Train layer followed by a frozen approach for the NN. The results indicate that the end-to-end configuration yields the highest accuracy, achieving 99.4% for the 25-class scenario and 89.9% for a 250-class scenario.

We introduce a method for generating quantum-jump trajectories using various quantum trajectory representations based on the master equation. This approach enables the straightforward simulation of these trajectories on standard quantum-jump frameworks, facilitating a direct comparison between different representations. We specifically examine a model featuring a two-level system strongly coupled to a bosonic field, analyzing three distinct quantum-jump formulations: the standard Caves-Milburn formalism, the quantum Langevin approach, and the quantum Langevin formalism. Our findings demonstrate that the probability of a quantum jump occurring within a specific time interval is consistent across all three representations. Furthermore, we show that the resulting trajectories accurately reproduce the evolution of the system's density operator as described by the corresponding master equation.

This study investigates the impact of plasmonic aluminum nanoparticle forms on the optical absorption within thin-film silicon solar cells. We evaluated three distinct morphologies: spherical nanoparticles, nanoparticle pillars, and a porous structure. The results indicate that porous aluminum offers the superior enhancement in absorption, followed by pillars and spheres, with the latter two showing comparable performance. This improved performance is primarily attributed to the scattering of light by the nanoparticles and the resulting increase in the effective optical path length. Furthermore, the porous structure uniquely mitigates reflection losses at the aluminum interface, thereby boosting absorption even in cells with minimal thickness.

We demonstrate that an enumeration construct, combined with a selection operator capable of filtering tuples based on specified properties, suffices to maintain first-order logic within the PTIME complexity class. This result is established without relying on the enumeration of solutions to property-satisfiability problems, thereby bypassing the need for a full logical theory of selection.

This study introduces a methodology and hardware co-design aimed at enhancing the energy efficiency of video identification systems powered by Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. The proposed approach involves decomposing the weight matrices of each LSTM layer into a hierarchical Tucker decomposition (HTD) format. This process reduces the computational burden of matrix multiplications by substituting them with a sequence of smaller operations. The research further analyzes the trade-off between classification accuracy and energy efficiency, offering a strategy to maintain performance levels while significantly cutting energy usage. The study concludes by detailing the hardware implementation of this energy-saving LSTM architecture using the FPGA-based Xilinx Kria KV260 platform. Experimental results indicate that the resulting energy-saving LSTM (ES-LSTM) achieves a 2.5x improvement in energy efficiency compared to a standard baseline, with only a marginal 1.5% drop in identification accuracy.

MAVLink, an open-source protocol developed by the British robotics firm ArduPilot, serves as the primary communication standard for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), facilitating data exchange between the aircraft and ground control stations. Despite its widespread adoption, the protocol lacks built-in security measures, leaving it vulnerable to various attacks. This paper introduces MAVSec, a security framework designed to secure UAV communications by integrating robust cryptographic techniques. The system employs a lightweight encryption algorithm, AES-GCM, to ensure data confidentiality and integrity, alongside a privacy-preserving mechanism based on the Diffie-Hellman key exchange to establish secure links. Additionally, MAVSec incorporates authentication protocols to verify the identity of connected entities. This security architecture is implemented within the PX4 Firmware, an open-source alternative to ArduPilot's flight control software. Finally, the paper outlines a series of experimental tests using a commercial quadcopter to validate the security and performance of the proposed protocol.

We introduce Kollaps, a distributed and dynamic framework designed to emulate the structure of a graph within a K-neighborhood. Kollaps operates by maintaining a compact, distributed representation of the neighborhood for each node, enabling local computation of metrics that would otherwise require global access to the original, centralized graph. This approach is particularly advantageous for large-scale graphs, as it eliminates the need to store the entire network in memory. Kollal supports a dynamic model that allows for real-time additions and removals of nodes and edges. We provide a formal definition of Kollal along with a detailed analysis of its space complexity and time requirements for both static and dynamic environments. Our evaluation demonstrates that Kollal is both space-efficient and scalable, and we validate its effectiveness through experiments on real-world datasets.

This study investigates the Newman-Penrose (NP) mapping, which translates a vacuum spacetime defined by a metric into a set of spin-coherent fields. We demonstrate that this mapping corresponds to a specific subclass of maps originating in twistor space. Furthermore, we reveal that the NP mapping is the initial instance of a novel class of maps, extending the known transformations from flat space to anti-de Sitter space.
